This road drives like a rod of iron from the Black Gates on into Gorgoroth, where it splits to encircle Orodruin.
Thousands of rough pairs of feet have marched, stood, and camped upon Udûn's broad central basin.
The heights above have been used for many purposes over the centuries; most recently to host a contingent of Easterling forces.
From here, a wary eye was kept on Anglach and the high bridge leading to it.
It is no coincidence that directly before Anglach affords the best view of all eastern Udûn.
An overseer may watch over the works below from here and, also, the road.
The doors were somehow wrenched asunder in the chaos and struggle that directly followed the fall of Sauron.
For what strange purpose was this platform used?
The lord of Durthang could survey his domain from this height -- and more.
Many fell weapons and great war-works have winded their way down this road, out of the great forges of Anglach.
Atop this steep ascent, countless rough, cruel weapons were wrought to arm the Dark Lord's immeasurable armies.
Servants bore goods and messages up this way to the fastness of Durthang.
Comings and goings along the Iron Road can be viewed with ease from this spot.
Being nearer to Barad-dûr, this path to Durthang was used for purposes of state and ceremony.
Great steam and water works were controlled from this point, which looked down onto the waste reservoirs below.

The Abyss of Mordath -- Explorer of the Black Pits
Discovered the Lithannon
Discovered Durshnúl, The Black Bridge
The Abyss of Mordath is home to both the condemned of Mordor and the Dark Lord's most carefully-guarded secrets.

Murpraush, the Hall of Spoiling, is where Sauron conducted the most vile of his sorceries. It was there he sought to equal the horrors of the first Dark Lord, Morgoth, and bring forth new and terrible creatures of his own imagining.

Thol Shíkug is a fortress of terror and death built into the very foundations of Barad-dûr. For those condemned to the Black Pits, it is known as the Screaming Deep -- for many an Orc, Man, and beast have met their ends at the hands of the Dark Lord and his most powerful servants within. What lies within this grim structure, none have ever returned to tell.

The Mordath, the Black Pits of Mordor, is a place devoid of hope. It is the foundation of Barad-dûr, an ever-deepening mine, and a pit of punishment for those that have failed the Dark Lord. Those who are cast into the Black Pits will never again behold the light of Middle-earth.

Glurnákh, The Pit of Greed, has long been the home to Fingar the Greedy, an ancient Worm of Angband. After devouring two of the Seven Rings, Fingar was captured and imprisoned beneath the Dark Tower to suffer evermore.

Glúrakul, The Pit of Frost, was once home to Hrímil Frost-heart, a cold-drake of the Grey Mountains. After Hrímil came to the dwarf-halls in the East and devoured one of the Seven Rings, she was captured and imprisoned beneath the Dark Tower. However, when Barad-dûr fell and the Mordath was shattered, she flew from her prison and escaped from Mordor.

Glúrghash, The Pit of Flame, was once the prison of Thostír the Rank, a great fire-drake of the East. After devouring one of the Seven Rings, he was captured by agents of Mordor and imprisoned beneath Barad-dûr. However, when the Mordath was split asunder, he flew from its shadowed depths and escaped the Land of Shadow.
You must explore the deepest depths of the Mordath to uncover all that was hidden away by Sauron.

Vive los acontecimientos de la Capa de Óxido y Cal.

Supiste de una serie de rumores entrelazados que inquietaban profundamente a los Hombres de Ciudad del Lago y de Valle. ¿Quién o qué es el Heraldo del Invierno? ¿Se ha cansado Vethúg Menteinvernal de sus tesoros en las Ered Mithrin, o ha aparecido otro de los Gúrzyul para sembrar temor y destrucción en el Norte?
Completa 'Heraldos de una Nueva Era'
La capa de óxido y cal
Hacia el final de la Tercera Edad, un viejo conflicto resurgió entre el Guerrero Lloroso y el Heraldo del Invierno.

Como la llegada de una gran tormenta, Vethúg Menteinvernal descendió sobre Erebor con furia y ansias de venganza. Muchos pueblos del Norte lucharon y cayeron, pero al final Vethúg sufrió una grave herida y huyó hacia las Montañas Grises derrotado.

La jefa de los cuervos, Arcah, llamó a sus aves de vuelta de sus pesquisas, pero no todas regresaron sanas. Rescataste a un cuervo herido perseguido por jóvenes dragonzuelos del frío en las laderas de Erebor y, poco después, pudo volar hasta la Colina de los Cuervos. Sin embargo, las noticias que trajo no auguraban nada bueno para los pueblos del Norte: Vethúg Menteinvernal había emprendido su vuelo desde las Montañas Grises y pronto descargaría su venganza sobre el Norte.

Cuando la oscuridad del Bosque Negro al fin comenzó a disiparse, Tárasánë, la Dama Verde, se reveló en Caras Tilion. En una poderosa visión, Tárasánë mostró que Vethúg Menteinvernal vendría a Erebor, pero solo como heraldo del verdadero Heraldo del Invierno. Aunque Tárasánë no mencionó su nombre, te dijo que ese Heraldo una vez sirvió la voluntad de Morgoth y ha habitado la Tierra Media desde los Días Antiguos. Regresaste al rey Thranduil con estas inquietantes noticias, y él envió mensaje a la Reina Regente y al Rey Bajo la Montaña.

Después de que el rey Thranduil viajara a Caras Tilion, fue atacado por las fuerzas de Karazgar. Thranduil combatió a Karazgar en duelo singular, pero antes de que la batalla se inclinara a su favor, despertó fuera de Felegoth como de un trance. Temiendo que Karazgar buscara el poder de la misteriosa Dama Verde, Thranduil te envió a Caras Tilion para desafiarlo. Descubriste las secuelas de un combate entre Elfos y Hombres de Mordor, pero Karazgar solo dejó óxido a su paso. La Dama Verde se manifestó, pero sus intenciones siguen sin estar claras. ¿Qué poderes posee? ¿Es de la misma estirpe que el Cazador de las Tierras Brunas?

Finalmente, Karazgar reveló sus planes en el Viejo Esgaroth. Los restos destrozados de los jóvenes dragonzuelos del frío que sus agentes capturaron en los confines de las Ered Mithrin yacían expuestos entre los huesos de Smaug el Dorado. Era un ardid para enfurecer a los grandes dragonzuelos al servicio del Heraldo del Invierno y desatar su ira contra los Elfos, Hombres y Enanos del Norte. Un drake moribundo te reveló que uno de los suyos escapó a la ira de Karazgar en el Viejo Esgaroth y voló a las Ered Mithrin para advertir al Heraldo del Invierno. A pesar de los esfuerzos de los líderes del Norte, parece que el vil complot del Guerrero Lloroso ha tenido éxito.

Supiste que los agentes del Guerrero Lloroso habían estado reuniendo jóvenes dragonzuelos del frío en Ciudad del Lago bajo la cobertura de la noche. Al escuchar una conversación entre un contrabandista y un siervo de Karazgar, descubriste que Karazgar no solo quería usar a los dragonzuelolings para reforzar su fuerza, sino también para enviar un mensaje al Heraldo del Invierno y al propio Norte. También descubriste que Karazgar viajó a Eryn Lasgalen, aunque sus propósitos siguen sin quedar claros.

Después de que revelaste al rey Thorin que Vethúg Menteinvernal busca poner sitio a Erebor, él se preparó para reunir a las fuerzas del Norte y rechazar al legendario dragón frío. Temiendo que Vethúg sirva en verdad a un poder mayor, ha decidido darle muerte y vengar a sus ancestros que moraron en las Ered Mithrin. Tras un intento de humor poco acertado, el rey Thorin te pidió que llevaras sus mensajes a los líderes del Norte. Aunque algunos ofrecieron ayuda de mala gana, todo indica que el Norte permanece unido contra los siervos del Enemigo.

A petición del rey Thorin, buscaste una audiencia con el rey Thranduil. Le ofreciste un gesto de paz en nombre de los enanos de Erebor y le advertiste que Karazgar rondaba ahora el reino de los Elfos. El rey Thranduil reunió a sus exploradores, y tú ayudaste a guiarlos para buscar a Karazgar bajo el dosel de Eryn Lasgalen. ¿Qué revelarán sus pesquisas?

Aunque supo que Karazgar podía haber regresado a Caras Tilion, el rey Thranduil debió atender otro asunto. La Vieja Madre, Iphantemel, había reaparecido en Torech Emel, y al fin había llegado la hora de vengar la destrucción de Caras Tilion y la corrupción del Bosque Negro. Lejos de ser la enemiga robusta a la que Thranduil enfrentó antaño, Iphantemel estaba ahora vieja y deforme por sus excesos, y parecía acoger la muerte con alivio. Las arañas fueron por fin purgadas de Eryn Lasgalen, pero solo porque Ungwetári llamó a su prole hacia las Ephel Dúath con algún terrible propósito. El rey Thranduil se volvió suspicaz respecto a los motivos de Karazgar para viajar a Caras Tilion y juró buscarlo con una pequeña compañía de Elfos.

Temiendo que las visiones de la Dama Verde te hubieran confundido, el rey Thorin III te aconsejó buscar el consejo del rey Thranduil. A su vez, el rey Thranduil te sugirió acudir ante la Dama Galadriel y el poder del Espejo. Tras viajar a Caras Galadhon, la Dama Galadriel no creyó posible que Karazgar hubiese llegado tan al sur y entrado en las ruinas de Dol Guldur sin ser visto por los Galadhrim. Consultó el Espejo, pero nuevamente no vio indicio alguno de Karazgar en Dol Dhannen, el nombre que ahora recibe Dol Guldur. Aun así, sintió que algo escapaba a su visión y meditó largamente sobre lo que debía hacerse.

Tras mucha deliberación, la Dama Galadriel viajó a Dol Dhannen junto al señor Celeborn, el rey Thranduil, Sigileth y tú. La exploración de las ruinas de Dol Dhannen casi resultó infructuosa hasta que descubriste un pequeño pasaje que descendía a los túneles sombríos de Gostador. Tal como la Dama Galadriel esperaba, no encontraste a Karazgar en sus profundidades. Sin embargo, un gran mal aún se cernía allí, y presenciaste vagas impresiones de los tratos finales entre Karazgar y Sauron en Dol Guldur. Supiste que a Karazgar se le prometió el dominio entero del Norte una vez sus pueblos fueran expulsados, y que el Guerrero Lloroso podría someter o destruir a cualquiera de los dragones que aún vivieran en ese reino. También supiste que Hrímil Corazónhelado desafió a Sauron y devoró uno de los Anillos de los Enanos por despecho. Tras estas revelaciones, regresaste a Erebor e informaste al rey Thorin III de que Karazgar podría seguir al acecho.

Tras saber que Vethúg Menteinvernal vuela hacia Erebor, los pueblos del Norte comenzaron a preparar sus defensas con determinación. Ayudaste a los pueblos de Valle, Ciudad del Lago y Felegoth a alistarse para la batalla y defender sus hogares.

Tras la batalla en Erebor, los cuervos revelaron que Karazgar había perseguido al herido Vethúg Menteinvernal hasta las Montañas Grises. Para desdicha de los suyos, el rey Thorin III decretó que no se emprendiera ninguna expedición a las Montañas Grises, pues tanto él como Erna y Thranduil consideraban prudente no involucrarse en el conflicto entre Karazgar y Vethúg ahora que ambos habían abandonado el Norte.

Pese a su edicto, el rey Thorin III ha oído rumores inquietantes sobre una expedición para reclamar Thikil-gundu, el Bastión de Acero, de manos de los dragones y orcos de las Montañas Grises. Todos los enanos a los que hablaste negaron tal expedición, pero Thorin III no quedó convencido. Tras hablar con el aventurero Dori y saber que no tenía intención de desafiar al Rey Bajo la Montaña, te pidió hablar con Nori sobre un grupo de enanos visto en los cofres durante la noche. Para sorpresa de todos en Erebor, Nori partió y lideró una expedición hacia las Montañas Grises. El rey Thorin III estaba furioso, pero no violaría su propio edicto. El destino de la expedición a Thikil-gundu recaía ahora en Nori.

Mientras el resto del Norte se preparaba para la llegada de Vethúg Menteinvernal, Dís convocó al rey Thorin III a la Colina de los Cuervos. Para su sorpresa, la jefa de los cuervos, Arcah, había regresado de tierras lejanas y deseaba hablar con el nuevo Rey Bajo la Montaña. Tras acordar honrar los antiguos lazos entre sus pueblos, Arcah envió a sus cuervos por todas partes para espiar tanto a Karazgar como a Vethúg Menteinvernal.

Discovered Bekâr-mazal, the Arming-chamber
Long before the great cold-drake Vethúg Wintermind froze the halls of Thikil-gundu, the Longbeards delved the Steel Keep in the depths of the Grey Mountains.

You have discovered the Smithies of Kall-khebâb. Once a great craft-hall of Thikil-gundu, the old smithies of the Steel Keep have been seized by the Orcs of Gundabad in service to the brood of Vethúg Wintermind and his forebear, Hrímil Frost-heart.

You have discovered Bekâr-mazal, the Arming-chamber. Despite housing many weapons and tools of war, the great armoury of Thikil-gundu did not avail the Dwarves of the Steel Keep in the battle against Vethúg Wintermind.

You have discovered Balb-gundu, the Frostdelf. One of the only remaining delvings of Thikil-gundu, the Frostdelf once comprised much of Thikil-gundu until a great portion of it collapsed into the Depths of Akhatâr. It now serves as the lair of Athramóth, the mate of Vethúg Wintermind and mother of countless dragon-kind in the Grey Mountains.
You have discovered Zashar-tûmun, the Ruin-dwellings. Once a great dwelling-hall of the Dwarves of Thikil-gundu, Zashar-tûmun has fallen to ruin.

You have discovered the Feast-house of Amrâg-zahar. In the course of many long years, both the Longbeards and Zhélruka enjoyed great feasts and merriment in Amrâg-zahar before the fall of the Steel Keep. When Durin's Folk sought to return to Thikil-gundu, it was there Vethúg Wintermind waited in ambush and descended to slay Dáin, Frór, and countless other Longbeards.

You have discovered the Lore-trove of Afhân-binnîn. A great hall of lore lost to the Longbeards and Zhélruka. Many of its works have been brought to ruin, either by time or by the breath of cold-drakes, but a few pieces of note may still remain in the shadows of Afhân-binnîn.
You have discovered the Depths of Akhatâr. These shadowed pits have not been mapped by any living dwarf, but who knows what could dwell in the depths of the Grey Mountains?
You have discovered Razûkh-zahari, the Room of Rain. A great underground river travels beneath the Grey Mountains, and passes through a carefully-delved crack above the Room of Rain.
You have discovered Thikil-nesad, the Steel Seat. Once the seat of countless Kings of the Longbeards and Zhélruka, Thikil-nesad was abandoned when the Steel Keep fell to Vethúg Wintermind.

You have discovered the Hoarding-vault of Immêsh-khalt. Frozen beneath a layer of impenetrable ice, the Hoarding-vault of Immêsh-khalt is lined with the combined wealth of Durin's Folk and the Zhélruka.

How they jumped! Gandalf was astonished, as they all shouted with surprise and delight.
'This is not my adventure. I may look in on you again before it is over, for I have some rather pressing business to attend to.'
'A very good tale!' said Beorn. 'The best I have heard for a long while. Let's have something to eat!'
The dwarves' beards quivered as they listened, for they knew that soon they must venture into the Mirkwood.
'I hope you like the look of it. Now you must send back Beorn's ponies that you have borrowed.'
There, far away was the Lonely Mountain on the edge of the horizon. Snow remaining on its highest peak, unmelted and gleaming.

'Wargs range far and fast. They could be on you before you even knew they were there. If you travel at night, you might be wise to keep a camp-fire going. It would give away your position, but the wargs could smell you out anyway. They do not fear fire, but they do not like it, and it might deter them from testing you. Then again it might not. I will speak true: it is a tough decision. Perhaps it is best to travel only by day, after all.' - Ragnild of the Bear-folk

Enemies of the Vales
Conquer the many enemy encampments in the Vales of Anduin.
Conquer the many enemy encampments in the Vales of Anduin.

Ugúrz established his camp of Brafulug to prey upon traders on the road, believing his Orcs would be far enough from Lothlórien to escape the notice of the Elves. This would prove to be a miscalculation.

Wargs have often ventured into the Beorning-lands over the years, but those that dwell at Ylgraf today are larger and more ferocious than others of their kind. These wargs come from Gundabad, and they slink among the rocks to the north of the Beorninghús, waiting to attack Grimbeorn and his kin.

Côs Braen stands along the southern edge of Laerlad, home to the Ungoledain and their venomous kin. They hate Grimbeorn and his folk with a sickly passion, and would wipe out Beornings and Gauredain alike if they were given the chance.

Dredging machines stand in the mud of the Gladden Fields, once manned by Orc and half-orc, but now abandoned. A great hole was delved at Sharkey's Slough, and rumour has it that some prize was found in its depths. The half-orcs remain, seeking further treasures for themselves and not for their master. He remains silent, his thoughts elsewhere, and his servants at the Slough have received no message from him in some time.

Orcs searched the marshland for many weeks, operating from their camp of Lúlstrok in the north-western reaches the Gladden Fields. One of the great dredging machines stands there now, silent and still, but it once churned the earth during both day and night. Weapons, pieces of armour, and other trinkets were brought to Lúlstrok, but wherever these prizes may have gone in the time since is unknown.

The forester camp of Tríubad provided timber and other necessary supplies with which the Woodmen built their homes and the walls of their villages, but then the Taurogrim came. The Woodmen name them 'Thyrsir,' wood-demons, and they fear their blighted touch.
The Woodmen know Tríubad may be lost, but they do not spend time in mourning. Instead they seek adventurers to stop the Thyrsir from spreading the blight to other villages in Woodsedge.

A wet mist soaks the stones that lead to Shathur-munzu, the southernmost outpost of lost Khazad-dûm. The fortress is broken now, and dwarves have not lived there for many years. Shathur-munzu was the site of one of the bloodiest battles in the War of Dwarves and Orcs, and King Thráin did not hold it long.

The Beornings keep one eye on the Goblin-gate, for on this side of the mountains it is the primary way into, and out of, Goblin-town. During the last days of the War of the Ring, Orcs and goblins streamed through the Goblin-gate into the Vales of Anduin, raiding and burning peaceful Woodmen villages. Led by Grimbeorn the Old, the Beornings and Woodmen stood against the goblins and finally turned them back.
Now Goblin-town is quiet and there is little activity at the Goblin-gate, but the Beornings have not forgotten. They watch it still.

The peaceful Woodmen village of Waldfast has been destroyed by a goblin-host. Sentries are posted throughout the village, but their numbers are too few to explain the scope of the destruction. A cave behind the village might hold answers.

Following the final battles of the War of the Ring, a company of Orcs has established a tenuous foothold among the hills of Woodsedge. These are the Shapag-hai, and they have discovered they prefer to prey upon traders and travellers rather than warriors and soldiers. From their camp of Fil Sulmog they practice the art of pillaging, and have become quite good at it.

'They called it Orchost, but it is better known by another name: Goblin-town. Indeed, once it was a dwarf-delving, the High Hold of Zudrâligal. But the dwarves were driven out and the goblins made it their own. They stripped out most remnants of the dwarves, leaving only the barest traces of its former ancestry.' - Gandalf the Wizard

Once a beautiful lake, the Gladdenmere was wracked by upheavals during the War of the Last Alliance, and the land all about became a vast marshland, a perilous waste of dark pools and tangled grasses. The Gladdenmere has once again become accessible, but the path that allows curious travellers to reach it also allows passage for dangerous foes who might threaten the Wilderfolk of the Vales....

Protectors of the Vales

Home to Grimbeorn the Old and others of his family, the Beorninghús is generally closed to outsiders. During the final weeks of the War of the Ring, the Beornings found it necessary to take a more active role in the protection of the Vales of Anduin.
The sound of birdsong and the buzzing of dumbledors greet all who do approach the Beorninghús, but if they fail to ask Grimbeorn's permission, those are not the only sounds they will hear; Grimbeorn's wrath will be both loud and swift.
Explore the settlements of the Wilderfolk who live in the Vales of Anduin.
Explore the settlements of the Wilderfolk who live in the Vales of Anduin.

Located not far from the lost dwarf fortress of Shathur-munzu, the village of Arhaim is occupied by both Woodmen and Beornings. Together they maintain trade with the Elves and live a simple life in Duskenvale.
Gudule keeps a homestead in the Wolf-denes. 'This land has never been safe,' she says. 'We live too near to the mountains to sleep very soundly at night. But this is home.'

The Woodmen town of Hultvís was attacked during the closing weeks of the War of the Ring, but the Orcs and wargs were pushed back and eventually defeated by a united force of Beornings and Woodmen at the Battle of the Old Ford. Now the town seeks to rebuild and refortify, and seeks adventurers willing to assist with the recovery effort.
The Woodmen are a superstitious people, and at Hultvís you are sure to hear many legends and tales. These concern the beautiful and forlorn Maiden of Gladden, the spectral Vagári the Wanderer, hunger-crazed Old Mad Ubb, and the vanished Hól-budlan.

The village of Blómgard is found in Laerlad, not far from the fens of the Gladden Fields. The Woodmen there speak in hushed whispers of an unnatural darkness and a scuttling sound on the roofs of their homes. The leader of Blómgard, Odahild, has a reputation for honesty and she is not one to speak falsely, but others in the Vales of Anduin question if the tales from Blómgard are true. An adventurer might get to the bottom of it.
This Beorning watchpost guards the road into Duskenvale. Elves also keep watch on the southern road, but neither trusts the other to do it alone.

At Glándir, the Elves guard the road into Lothlórien, maintaining the safety of the Golden Wood. Lady Galadriel and Lord Celeborn have been known to visit the Elves here on occasion, seeking reports from the Vales of Anduin and bringing food and cheer with them to relieve the burden of those Elves who stay outside the bounds of Lórien.

The outpost of Vegbár allows the Beornings to keep watch over the road between the High Pass and the Old Ford, and to charge their toll of travellers and traders who go that way. Skalla commands at Vegbár, and despite his gruff exterior he cares deeply for his neighbours and worries for their safety.

The forester Ainhard keeps a homestead in the Wolf-denes, and his closest companions are his three hounds. He lives in fear of Orcs, goblins, and taurogrim, for he is no warrior. He relies upon the nearby Beorning outpost of Vegbár for protection.
Hodver keeps a homestead in the Wolf-denes, but he is ever ready to make for the Beorning outpost of Vegbár at the first sign of Orcs or wargs. 'I am no coward,' he says, 'but I am no fool, either.'

Much like Enedwaith on the far side of the Misty Mountains, the Vales of Anduin consist primarily of untamed wilderness, home to simple villages, hermits’ shelters, and only few roads. Most attempts to rule this wilderness have been short-lived and have long since fallen to ruin. You have done much to aid the Wilderfolk who live here, and made more secure a traditionally unsafe region.

Sites of the Vales

The Eyrie of the Great Eagles can only be reached by flying. It is the home of Gwaihir the Windlord and his folk, perhaps the oldest denizens of the Vales of Anduin. They have ranged far and wide from this high perch, and their coming has always signaled a change in the tides of fate: during Bilbo's adventures with Thorin and Company, when Gandalf the Grey suffered imprisonment by Saruman the White, and during the concluding hours of the War of the Ring.
If you should come to the Eyrie, it is always to your benefit to be as polite as you can be to your hosts. Not all of the Great Eagles are friendly with outsiders or unwinged folk.
Explore the many interesting locations to be found within the Vales of Anduin.
Explore the many interesting locations to be found within the Vales of Anduin.

The old keep of Avabárg stands on a low islet in the river. Once home to the Horse-folk that would come to be known as the Éothéod, Avabárg now stands empty except for a gloom that has seized the island, and the occasional Orc or goblin that thinks to fortify the island and make it his own.
Woodmen have tried to reclaim it over the years, but each attempt ended in failure, and now they treat it with superstitious fear.

The village of Rhosgobel, once the northernmost settlement of the Wood-elves and later the southernmost, is now home only to Radagast the Brown, one of the five Wizards. For a time he chose a nomadic life and dwelled in Ost Guruth, the Ruin-hold in the Lone Lands, but now he has returned to Woodsedge and seeks to combat the encroaching darkness.

The course of the Gladden did not always run as it does today. During the fighting at the close of the Second Age, Sauron sent forth his dark thought, attempting to rouse great evils to his cause. Whether such calamities responded to him is unknown, but around this time there were massive quakes in the Misty Mountains, shaking the dwarf-halls as far north as the High Pass.
The upheaval changed the course of the river, carrying sediment downstream and choking the Gladdenmere until its banks overflowed. Water poured over the cliff, flooding the valley and submerging its roads. In this way, the Gladden Fields became a wide marsh of reeds and dark pools. In time the level of the lake was restored, and the Gladden Falls became the narrow torrent it is today.

The High Pass through the Misty Mountains was treacherous and difficult to cross for many years, for both goblin raiders and stone-giants haunted the stones and crags and made travel difficult. When the Beornings arrived, the High Pass was cleared and they made an effort to push back these dangers. In return they charged a toll for passage, which other folk considered an unfair cost.
The High Pass was blocked during the War of the Ring, but today the Beornings have cleared it once again. Some say friendly stone-giants aided in this effort, but Grimbeorn's people will not say if this is so.

Hadhodiant was a mighty dwarf-bridge that served as the primary means of crossing the Anduin in the north, but it was broken shortly after the fall of Shathur-munzu in the Second Age. It was rebuilt, and indeed when the Great Alliance marched south to besiege Mordor, it was by way of the Hadhodiant that they crossed the Anduin.
But the bridge would not last. It broke in the middle, and when artisans from the Iron Hills were summoned to repair it, they were set upon by Orcs and every dwarf was slain. Over the course of centuries, stones of the bridge continued to fall into the river, until at last a tremendous flood swept away much of the ruin.
With the Hadhodiant destroyed, the Old Ford has come back into service as the primary means of crossing the Anduin in the north.

You found every stanza for a bit of doggerel the Woodmen of the Vales of Anduin tell to their children: the song of Old Mad Ubb. He sounds like a rather unpleasant creature... and also a little familiar.
You have learned much about the difficulties the Dwarves of Erebor faced in the North, and how those troubles often took a familiar shape: Dragon!

The lure of the ancient, lost city of Thafar-gathol has entranced the Zhélruka for much of their history, but despite many expeditions into the Grey Mountains it remains hidden, if it ever existed at all. You learned eight stanzas of a song extolling its virtues and its great wealth.

As you discovered in Thikil-gundu, the Steel Keep of the Grey Mountains, not all of Sauron's servants gave up hope at the defeat of their master. Karazgar, the Weeping Warrior, devised a plan to ensnare the Herald of Winter, claiming he would not suffer defeat as Sauron did.

You have learned a song which tells the history of Járnfast. Like the Dwarves of the Iron Hills who dwell there, its fortunes were built almost entirely upon the material that gives that region its name, and the song its refrain: iron hard, and iron cold.

You discovered a number of curious scratches in the hard stone of the Grey Mountains, and with much diligence you uncovered the full story. It is a cruel record of the dragon Smaug, and it tells of his growing fury and his desire for vengeance against the Dwarves of the North.

You have learned about the tradition of the Black Arrow, a tradition which was kept alive by lords of Dale for hundreds of years. How fortunate that it was so! For it was Bard's Black Arrow that at last slew the dragon Smaug.

You have learned a tale of the North that is all-too-familiar, for there are others like it. It is a tale of the enmity between Elves and dwarves, but in this case the tale goes further, to the healing between those folk, and that is a welcome difference.

Gorthad Nûr was once a place of solemn rest and peace, but without the maintenance of upkeep and cleaning provided by its keepers, it fell to filth and pestilence. Tombs throughout Middle-earth have long proven impossible for the vile kergrim to resist, and in Gorthad Nûr the creatures had time enough to develop their own rituals among the forgotten bones. They became the keepers of the Deep-barrow, and very few among the Free People remembered the place it once had been, before the desecration, before the rot.

Durante su esclavitud en Barad-dûr, los Hachetón eran considerados inferiores incluso al Orco más despreciable. A pesar de que los Hachetón soportaron la crueldad de los siervos del Enemigo, los antiguos odios entre enanos y Orcos no se olvidaron.

En las profundidades de Barad-dûr, toda reacción contra la crueldad de los Orcos se pagaba al precio más alto. Pero entre los Pueblos Libres de la Tierra Media, no existía tal dificultad y cada victoria contra ellos se reivindicaba con orgullo.

Desde el lejano sur llegó, trayendo miedo y fuego a cada costa que espiaba con su cristal. Su reinado era de sangre, y la extraía de todos los que vivían a la vista y al olor del Mar. ¿Fue esa la razón por la que Sauron le dio el anillo Khânto, que es el Dador de Dolor? Con el poder de él, el Despojador Proscrito no podía ser detenido, y su risa se extendía tierra adentro con vientos funestos; estaba entre los sirvientes más rápidos y crueles de Sauron.

Nadie puede decir qué barco lo llevó a la Tierra Media antes de que Númenor se perdiera, pero una vez que aceptó el regalo de Sauron, ya no podía ser contado entre los Hombres de esa tierra. Habitó en Thaurband, una fortaleza en el sur de Mordor, no lejos del Mar Interior. Desde esa fortaleza se extendió el miedo hacia él, dándole un nuevo título para reemplazar el nombre que ya no necesitaba. Se convirtió en la Languidez de Núrn, aunque no permaneció allí, y vagó por todas partes bajo el mando de Sauron.

Pocos entre los vivos lo han oído hablar, pero su rostro era conocido y temido. Lo llamaban el Suderon siniestro y, aunque los Hombres se acobardaban a su paso durante la Segunda Edad, durante la Tercera la leyenda de su maldad solo había crecido. En años posteriores fue él a quien Lhaereth la Manchada siguió en secreto a Dol Guldur, donde descubrió a Sauron y le ayudó a recuperarse, por un precio. ¿El Señor Oscuro le dio una recompensa o un castigo por esta falta a su Nazgûl? Pero eso fue mucho más tarde. Durante la Segunda Edad, el Suderon siniestro solo era conocido por ser paciente, leal y silencioso.

They called him the High Sorcerer of Harad, but for most of those who fought against Sauron it was just a name. He rarely left the dungeon fastnesses of Mordor, for he delighted in the working of foul rituals and the mastery of fell magics, and gave his thought to little else. But when the Dark Lord saw fit to send him forth, Men and Elves knew to give him a wide berth, or suffer. It was Mêbat he wore, the Mirth-eater, and wherever he went there was an end to laughter, and only the onset of grief.
Los Nueve

Una vez fue un gran rey en tierras lejanas al este, acostumbrado a gobernar y reacio a inclinar la rodilla ante cualquier otro. Pero luego vino un dador de regalos y un prometedor de poder, y al aceptar estos señuelos, el gran rey cambió. Ya no gobernaba sus tierras con misericordia, y tampoco permanecía en su propio reino. Se convirtió en el Daño de Rhûn, y con ese nombre llegó a ser conocido como el Daño de Rhûn, y en otros lugares.

The Great Alliance of Elves and Men stood in defiance of Sauron for long years of siege, but even their greatest heroes came to fear his deadliest servants. These were the Nazgûl, and their number was Nine.

Se movía rápidamente por el campo de batalla, persiguiendo a los guerreros que se atrevían a enfrentarse a él, cada vez menos a medida que avanzaba el asedio. Era el Jinete Maldito, y el sonido de su acercamiento convertía incluso la sangre más valiente en agua. En años posteriores comandaría ejércitos desde dentro de los muros de Dol Guldur, pero durante la Segunda Edad prefería luchar desde el lomo de su corcel negro, solo.

El más grande y temido de los Nueve, el Rey Brujo acechaba el campo de batalla pero rara vez, dejando las fortalezas de Mordor solo bajo la orden más urgente de Sauron. En años posteriores, el Señor de los Nazgûl levantaría de la nada la Tierra de Angmar, utilizándola para avanzar en el objetivo del Señor Oscuro de destruir el reino del norte de Arnor, pero al final de la Segunda Edad eso aún estaba lejos en las brumas del Tiempo. Durante el Asedio de Barad-dûr, el Rey Brujo se encontraba probando las debilidades de los ejércitos alineados contra su maestro, buscando el premio más valioso de todos: la información.

Era la Amargura de Khand y, con la bendición de Sauron, avanzó por las tierras no conquistadas y las reclamó para el Señor Oscuro. El anillo que se le otorgó se llamaba Adâsh, y muchos fueron los enemigos que creó, muchos los orgullosos guerreros que abatió. Encontraba gran alegría en provocar la guerra, y siempre lo había hecho, pero con el poder otorgado por Sauron, la Amargura de Khand se volvió cada vez más mortal, más implacable y más despiadada.

En días posteriores, la Espada Negra de Lebennin fue vista con frecuencia merodeando entre las colinas y los bosques de Gondor Occidental, infundiendo miedo en los corazones de los Hombres con su temible presencia y su espada mortal. Para aquellos pocos que no huían, sus palabras caían como miel en sus oídos reacios y los llevaban a cometer terribles actos de maldad. Esto pudo haber demostrado ser su peor y más eficaz arma.

'They call it the Harrowing,' one young soldier in Echad Uial whispered to his captain. 'The Orcs battle for control of the lowest level of the city, and neither faction can wrest the upper hand away from the other.'
'The Harrowing, eh?' his captain answered. 'What do you call it?'
The young soldier looked first one way and then the other, and lowered his voice.
'Orc fight,' he whispered. His captain nodded, and handed the soldier a whetstone.
'Good enough for me,' he said.

Años de guerra implacable y asedio redujeron las áridas pero fértiles llanuras de Mordor a un yermo, y bajo la amenaza constante de la maldad de Sauron durante la Tercera Edad, jamás se recuperaron. Muchas fueron las fortificaciones levantadas por la Gran Alianza en los últimos años de la guerra, pero tres mil años después solo quedaban ruinas y fragmentos, un recordatorio de que toda gloria se desvanece y hasta la victoria puede no perdurar.
'The real treasure, if you ask me, was the spiders we slew along the way!' - Atli Spiderbane
'You can find treasure anywhere! It might not even look like treasure, and still be valuable.' - Covadil, Scholar of Gondor
'What did you find? Spiders? Ah, tell me more. It sounds to me as if our work is not yet finished, my friend!' - Atli Spiderbane

The baths of Minas Ithil were once a place to rest and relax, and the people who lived here scrubbed away the dirt and the grime of their daily lives, sinking into waters of contentment. Now the baths are empty of all good folk, haunted by shades of evil.
'Is there anything more sad to the heart than a garden dead and twisted? So it was with Ithilien, and already we work to restore my land's beauty. Perhaps it can be the same here.' - Prince Faramir
The Dome of Evening has been sealed away for years uncounted, and for purpose unknown.

Most of Minas Ithil's treasures were already looted, either by good folk fleeing from the city in advance of its several falls, or by forces of evil in search of artifacts and gold. The relics that remain have been corrupted by the long residence of the Nazgûl and their minions, and now Bâr Maenath holds only ill fortune for the few treasure-seekers who dare explore there.
Once a place of feasting and good cheer, the Wracking-hall has not known a meal free of terror for countless years. Now it is a den of evil, and only horrors sup there.
The Shadow-roost of Gath Daeroval is home to Khatlob, the great brood-mother who birthed the vile flying mounts used by the Nazgûl in pursuit of the aims of Sauron.
Barad Cúron rises from the top of the city, a place of mystery much-coveted by each of the Masters of Mordor.
Ugrukhôr's forces have pushed into Minas Morgul and established the encampment of Zhar Skator upon the Circle of Wrath.
The sprawling encampment of Zhar Dushgoi was established by Gothmog's Orcs who gather what defenses they can to hold the Circle of Wrath from Ugrukhôr's forces.

Barad Angarth has been reclaimed from the Orcs, and now it serves the White Company as a foothold in the city. Further such towers may better serve the reclamation, but they will first need to be taken from the foes that hold them.
Explore the many places of fear and dread that can be found within Minas Morgul.
Explore the many places of fear and dread that can be found within Minas Morgul, the Dead City.

The Circle of Mirth above which stood Barad Arthir has become the Circle of Despair, haunted by spirits and a place of great danger for Faramir's White Company, which seeks to restore the city. That goal remains far-off, but every step taken is a step closer, and with the spirits driven out of Barad Arthir, perhaps more victories will soon follow.
The gauntmen walk in Roz Dagalur, and few only know the way inside. Fewer still know the way out.

They say the forge works still, but the hands of men touch it not. In Búrzangh some ghostly power takes command, seeking to craft some relic of ancient days, but none among the living can say what artifact the spirits desire to create.
The smell of decaying flesh fills the Hall of Rot, and wights stalk among chambers once home to light and life. But those days are gone, and King Elessar is uncertain if they can ever return.

The dusty paths between the shelves of Ghashan-kútot are walked by an unnatural force. It answers to the name Dolguzigir, but few only have seen the Accursed Sage. It is said he can drape himself in whatever form he wishes, but he is not a Man, and if he appears so it is only in answer to his whim. He is eager to learn the story of any who stray into the Hall of Black Lore, eager almost to the point of sickness, and he does not wish for any to leave... uncollected.

Minstrels and poets flocked to Minas Ithil when Gondor was at its height, and the lamps were lit in the Song-house of Lindalírë long into the night. But the Night proved darker and more insidious, and with the coming of the Witch-king the theatre is host only to the Dead.

Barad Orhant once overlooked the Circle of Skill in Minas Ithil, but now the view has changed. That tier is now the Circle of Sorrow, and it is home only to the Dead. So too was the Tower of the Treegarth, but it has been seized for the use of the White Company. Perhaps it will be the same for the Circle of Sorrow.

Barad Elenath, the Star-gazers' Spire, was once a place of study and learning. From its great height the scholars of the city spent night after night studying the moon and the stars, but that was long ago. The merrevail of Lhaereth the Stained claimed this tower, and have only just been driven away. The tower serves now as a foothold for the White Company's reclamation of Minas Morgul.

It was at Bâr Nírnaeth, the Houses of Lamentation, where the Nazgûl worshipped their master Sauron. Many were the dark and profane rituals that were conducted here in his name, and the mark of those terrible evils remain still upon every one of their buildings and courtyards.
Scouting Thuringwath

Falch Gurth, the Deathly Cleft, was a secret path leading back into the southern Ephel Dúath. It was hewn by the Nazgûl when they first conquered Minas Ithil during the Second Age, and hidden by concealing spells that could not be broken while Sauron survived. It was visible only to the Dark Lord and his servants, but now, with its master defeated, it is revealed to all as the passage to the long-hidden gorge of Thuringwath.
Explore the dark and dreadful sites that lie within Thuringwath.
Explore the dark and dreadful sites that lie within Thuringwath.

Atop a massive underground tomb rests Aufaltor, the Fane of the Eye. Without number are those counted amongst the Dead of Aufaltor, for it was here the servants of the Nazgûl laid the lifeless bodies of those they deemed unworthy of the dark rites of Agath-kali, Mistress of Lamentation, in Bâr Nírnaeth.

Long before Ufurok became a monument to the Gaunt-lords, it was a fortress erected in defence of Bâr Nírnaeth. It was Laugdursh, the Dire Span over which the Nazgûl and their most unfortunate victims travelled to the Houses of Lamentation. It fell into disuse once the Nazgûl adopted fell-beasts as their winged mounts in the Third Age of the world.

It was to Ufurok, the Dreadfast, that the Witch-king of Angmar drew five of the mightiest Gaunt-men of the Elder Days. It was his will to empower them, crafting them into terrible, twisted reflections of the Wizards whose arrival in Middle-earth threatened the Dark Lord. The fell sorceries of the Witch-king unmade them and reshaped them into the Gaunt-lords. These were their names, and their number was five: Ivar the Blood-hand, Thadúr the Ravager, Ferndúr the Virulent, Drugoth the Death-monger, and Gortheron the Doom-caller.
With many of their number too fearful to press into the shadows of Thuringwath, the Rangers of Ithilien make camp at Torgris, the Hidden Cleft, a small crack in the heart of Falch Gurth.

But Sauron's forces were also united, taken from many different pits of evil, and forged into a singular fighting force. Their bonds were made not of friendship but of fear... fear of their dark master. Still it proved effective.' - Isildur

'I am grieved to hear that the Orcs remain still in this world. They were a fearsome foe when we fought against Sauron, cruel and deadly, without an ounce of mercy. Many of my friends and soldiers perished in their encampments. The one called Mokh Shapat remained for years, despite our attempts to eradicate it.' - Isildur

'Mokh Darga was a large encampment from which the Orcs launched many attacks upon Adambel. My father himself turned away several of these assaults, deeds which inspired not just the men under his command but also proved an inspiration to me and to my brother. Alas for Anárion!'
'Barthost, you say? I do not remember that name. Perhaps Gultháva's enchantment has not yet released me from its grip.' - Isildur

'It was a camp of evil men, sworn to serve Sauron. I never set foot inside, but I know the forces of Sauron festered in their malice within its bounds, and set forth with hatred in their hearts, intending to defeat the Great Alliance.' - Isildur
'Shades drifted within Angathrai, given cruel purpose by Mordorrim cultists and the will of Sauron. Let us not speak of them.' - Isildur

'Díngarth was the most secure location of the Free Peoples, built at the beginning of the siege and repeatedly assailed and rebuilt over the ensuing years. Near the end it was mostly emptied, kept as a last redoubt in the event that the forward forces of the Alliance were overwhelmed and forced to retreat. My sons greatly enjoyed making life difficult for Ontamo, the master of the fortifications at Díngarth, despite my chiding of them for it.' - Isildur
'Adambel was the forward encampment of Men, from whence my father Elendil and my brother Anárion and I commanded our armies. It was the nearest to Barad-dûr we deemed it wise to set camp.' - Isildur

'It was Amon Fuin, the Gloom-hill, the last remaining major fortification held by Sauron’s forces beyond the Dark Tower itself. The Mordorrim conducted sacrifices and other rituals behind the walls of that fortress, and many were the soldiers of the Great Alliance we lost to their deadly excursions.' - Isildur
'The shades and spirits of Matum Graz lingered alongside the dead that walk, and they nursed hatred for the living in their evil hearts. I do not wish to speak of them now.' - Isildur

As Gultháva's enchantment fades, Isildur comes to remember the events at the close of the Second Age, when Mordor was besieged.

'Dol Naeg was the name of a rocky spur on the north slope of Amon Amarth. It is a place of great sadness for me, for that is where my father died. It is also where I obtained an artifact of Sauron that brought me only sorrow and grief. Would that I had never stood there!' - Isildur
'I know the tunnel of Halroth, but I never ventured inside. Glorfindel of the Bright Company knows of that place. Let him speak of it, if he will.' - Isildur

'Barad-dûr, the tower of Sauron, was built not by his servants but by Númenórean hands. He has bent it to his evil, and it stood as a cruel mockery to my people. He remained within for the long years of the siege, content to outlast us, but it was not to be.' - Isildur

'The wargs of Baur Kasak were feared by all the men under my command, for the beasts could move at incredible speed across the plains, seizing an unwary soldier with their powerful jaws and charging away in moments. Many of my soldiers insisted upon being accompanied on the plains by an Elf of Gil-galad's forces, for only their swift bows could dissuade the advance of such creatures.' - Isildur

'Echad-in-Edhil was the forward encampment of the Elves, and it was where Gil-galad and his household dwelt for much of the siege. From this camp, the High Elves of the Bright Company undertook many dangerous excursions on the plains before Barad-dûr and against Sauron's servants.' - Isildur

Few of the Rangers of Ithilien have braved the hills of Rath Dúath. There upon an overlook, those few have established the small encampment of Taen Orwath.

This western gate from the valley could be shut in case of trouble, preventing access to Ithilien. This proved a fairly frequent occurrence during the long and tumultuous history of Gondor. Annon Morgul has been damaged by war, and is now a ruin.

Countless bones fill the Deep-barrow of Gorthad Nûr, an unholy ossuary carved into the rock of the mountains. Tombs and shrines remain, but they have been desecrated by dark arts. Kergrim howl among the forgotten statues, hungry for flesh, but few other sounds can be heard.

Prince Faramir's White Company established the camp of Echad Uial on the eastern side of Rath Dúath, intending to marshal expeditions into Minas Morgul itself. But they have spent much attention maintaining the watch on the Dread Door of Fennas Gost, and there are never enough adventurers willing to face the Dead City.

The warg dens of Râkh Mathán extend up into the hills surrounding Rath Dúath, and the creatures' wailing howls strike fear even into the brave hearts of Faramir's Rangers. Especially the Rangers, for they have experienced much grief at the teeth and claws of the beasts during the last several months, as the wargs have ranged further from their dens at the command of their Orkish masters.

The Orc encampment of Banám Lugaun sees a great deal of activity during both night and day, serving as a waypoint of sorts for servants of evil on their way to one place or another within Imlad Morgul.

The merrevail roost of Shakam Moz watches over both Rath Dúath and Lhingris from the high peak, and the minions of Lhaereth the Stained prove a terror for all who are forced to travel in those valleys.

Anborn, Ranger of Ithilien, has established the camp of Estolad Lân on the western side of Rath Dúath. From there he seeks to carry out the commands of Prince Faramir of Ithilien, though the camp rests nearly beneath the very shadow of Minas Morgul.

This is the main bridge over the Morgulduin. It has been destroyed and rebuilt several times throughout the history of Rath Dúath, but now it stands anew, carrying the primary road to Minas Morgul across the rushing waters.

The Filth-well of Eithel Gwaur is located at the source of the Morgulduin, and appears to be the cause of that river's foul contagion. It is not known when the cavernous cistern first fell prey to its corruption and disease, but the river has not been called Ithilduin for many years, and its clean waters are only the faintest memory now.

This is the first of the stairs climbed by Frodo Baggins, Samwise Gamgee, and the creature Gollum by which they intended to gain access to the Land of Mordor. The stairs are tall and steep, and while the climb is straight and without turns, the steps are uneven and treacherous. The stairs are cut into the flanks of the Ephel Dúath and climb from the floor of the valley up to the pass itself, on the western side of Cirith Ungol.
Explore the many dreadful and worrisome locations to be found within Cirith Ungol.
Explore the many dreadful and worrisome locations to be found within Cirith Ungol.

The Ungoledain have come a long way overland across Middle-earth, following a call only they can hear, and they have established the resting-place of Cadar Skûs in the mountains. Is their long journey finally near its end?

None have seen beyond the entrance to Remmorchant, the Net of Darkness, for that is the deepest and most subterranean of Ungwetári's tunnels, the pitted and sunless abyss into which she retreated after her unexpected injury at the hands of Samwise Gamgee and the point of Sting, the Gondolin-forged blade wielded by both Bilbo and Frodo Baggins, and later by the terrified but deadly gardener of Bag End.
Ungwetári knew nothing of those hobbits or the lineage of that blade, but she remembers the pain of that encounter, and it has built in her a white-hot and blinding rage. In Remmorchant she broods upon her wound, and festers in her hatred.

The forest of Taurlingol has become spider-infested, a place of webs and unnatural voices. If the Ungoledain can understand the chittering of their idols, they are unwilling to share its meaning. This is probably a good thing.

Uruks following the commands of Rukhor the Pale Herald have established this camp atop the Winding Stair, west of Cirith Ungol. It seems they have run afoul of the Ungoledain and spiders ranging out of Taurlingol and Torech Ungol, which is unsurprising. Expectedly, some uruks have also fallen to infighting among themselves and with other Orc-bands creeping down from the tower and through the pass.

The pass of Cirith Ungol was rarely left unguarded, but few only would dare to make the crossing while the Orcs of the tower could spy on them from above. The worse and far greater danger was spoken of only in whispers, for few good folk knew even rumour of it. Some dark terror dwelled in the tunnel of Torech Ungol, through which the path must lead. Even should a traveller make it safely through the web-haunted passage, the tunnel gave way to a chasm open to the sky but riddled with cave-mouths on each cliffside from which any foe might have the advantage of surprise. No tactician would advise taking that road.
It was the favourite hunting-ground of Ungwetári, last daughter of Ungoliant, and only the very foolish or the very desperate should go that way.

This second stair begins high above the valley floor, and unlike the Straight Stair it weaves back and forth along the cliffside, a great chasm yawning to one side. At the top of the stairs, a dark cleft leads onward to the entrance of Torech Ungol and the horrors within.
Mablung has established the small camp of Echad Taerdim at the top of the Straight Stair, and he intends to use it as a base from which to mount small expeditions into nearby Cirith Ungol.

Quests of Minas Morgul
Complete quests in Minas Morgul.
The Circle of Wrath is home to several warring Orc-factions, and by your efforts they have been dealt a serious blow.

The name may be of recent invention, for the Circle of Madness has become infested with merrevail sent by Lhaereth, Lady of Blight, and her madness is known to ally and foe alike. She commanded them with a single-minded purpose, and you stood against her minions with equal determination. In time, this tier of the city may reacquire its original appellation: Circle of Wisdom.

The Circle of Sorrow has not welcomed the living for many years and has become home only to the Dead. Through your efforts, you have brought the warmth of life back to this tier of the city. Such warmth will not stay, but you have wielded it as a weapon against the spirits of this place, a warning that the city belongs no longer to them.

It was the command of King Elessar that every tier of the city be cleansed of evil, and Faramir wished to see it done, but the continued presence of Gothmog's servants in the Circle of Despair proved especially troubling for the Prince of Ithilien. 'Once this was the Circle of Mirth,' he mused, 'but today the only laughter to be heard on this level is cruel and full of mockery. Will it ever be quieted? I cannot say.'

Many are the mysteries confronting Prince Faramir and his Rangers on the Circle of Death, uppermost tier of Minas Morgul. Still they stand against the forces of evil that seek to preserve the vile secrets of the Dead City.
Complete many quests in the reclamation of Minas Ithil.

El príncipe Durin ha convocado una asamblea, en la que se decidirá el destino de Gundabad. Aún así, ni los planes más elaborados pueden hacer frente a la fuerza de un dragón desencadenado, y Hrímil Corazónhelado dirige a sus ejércitos contra los enanos antes de que estén del todo preparados. Con un aliado inesperado a tu lado, asciendes a la cumbre de la montaña para enfrentarte al más feroz de los enemigos: la Señora de Gundabad en persona, con el destino de Gundabad y de los enanos pendiendo de un hilo.
Con Gundabad retomado, el príncipe mira ahora al futuro y a las conquistas todavía por venir...
Completa 'El Legado de Durin, Epílogo'
Completa 'El Legado de Durin, Capítulo 1'
El legado de Durin y las pruebas de los Enanos
Descubre la historia de 'El legado de Durin y las pruebas de los Enanos'

Mientras los enanos avanzan hacia Gundabad, cada miembro del Gabil'akkâ es llamado a la batalla, pero no todos son idóneos para la tarea. Eskil Pulgarsangriento, aprendiz del escultor Stáli el Tallador, es uno de estos enanos, y cuando encuentra dificultades en las profundidades de la Hendidura Profunda necesita tu ayuda no solo para escapar de las garras de los orcos, sino también de su aprendizaje con Stáli.

Los misterios abundan mientras exploras los confines de Gundabad, encontrándote extraños encantamientos tanto en el Foso de Faucespétreas como en las cumbres nevadas de Câr Bronach. Tus aliados y tú habéis perserverado valientemente contra los planes de los guerreros hobotrasgos y los cultistas Angmarim, pero un amenazante y desconocido poder envuelve el Hogar de la Montaña, aunque tanto su fuente como su propósito todavía son desconocidos para ti.

El Gabil'akkâ sufre una derrota descorazonadora con el ataque de Gorgar al puesto de avanzada principal de los enanos en Gundabad, pero las muertes de sus soldados no son el único arma que blande contra el príncipe Barbiluengo. Empuña un poderoso martillo hecho de mithril, lo que supone un golpe aplastante contra los enanos. '¿Eres lo mismo que yo?' le pregunta a Durin antes de marcharse, y aunque el príncipe desdeña la pregunta, le perturba.
Durin te ha pedido que te aventures todavía más hacia el interior de Gundabad con una doble misión: vengar a aquellos perdidos a manos de Gorgar y frustar los esfuerzos de los Angmarim que están profanando los lugares considerados sagrados por los enanos.

El Gabil'akkâ ha capturado a un trasgo llamado Glúrkub, un importante consejero de Gorgar antes del comienzo de la Guerra de las Tres Cumbres. Las palabras que ha pronunciado desde su cautiverio hacen temblar los cimientos de las convicciones del príncipe Durin en su causa y en sí mismo, pero todavía hay esperanza. Si Glúrkub dice la verdad, Gorgar se reúne con Hrímil Corazónhelado en los Altos de las Nubes, y cuando lo hace no lleva el martillo de mithril. Durin quiere aprovechar esa oportunidad, aunque lo invaden la cólera y la desconfianza.

En las profundidades de Gundabad, se revelan secretos que hacen temblar la determinación del principe Durin, pero con tu ayuda consigue dominar sus sentimientos y acepta el complicado legado de sus antepasados.

El príncipe Durin reúne a sus tropas para la batalla, ¡y comienza la Guerra de las Tres Cumbres! La lucha tiene sus idas y venidas, mientras los orcos llevan a cabo una feroz defensa y los primeros éxitos por parte del Gail'akkâ no son suficientes para asegurar la victoria completa. Las tensiones estallan entre varios clanes de los enanos a pesar de su enemigo commún, y las discusiones entre los Barbiluentos, Zhélruka y Hachetones amenazan con debilitar el esfuerzo de la guerra. Finalmente, Durin marcha hacia las puertas de Gundabad para enfrentarse a Gorgar, pero justo cuando la victoria parecía asegurada un terrible rugido resuena desde las alturas: Hrímil Corazónhelado se ha liberado de su gélida presión en el Yunque Invernal, y reclama la soberanía de Gundabad. Durin ordena la retirada, pero jura no ceder el Hogar de la Montaña a este nuevo intruso, o a cualquier otro.
El siguiente capítulo comenzará con el príncipe Durin, localizado bien en Zarkul-sulûn durante la Guerra de las Tres Cumbres o en Annâk-khurfu en el Valle Ancestral.

Corren inquietantes rumores que afirman que Gorgar el Despiadado, hijo de Bolg y hermano de Mazmog, se ha nombrado a sí mismo 'Señor de Gundabad', obligan a Glóin a enviar un mensaje de advertencia al príncipe Durin Yelmo de Piedra. La advertencia es agradecida pero no atendida: nada parará el asalto de Durin a Gundabad. Ha hecho llamar a los ejércitos de los enanos para que desciendan al Valle Ancestral y así prepararse para el conflicto, incluyendo a los supervivientes de la Guarnición de Hierro. Estos valientes enanos intentarán conseguir la victoria que no lograron en Moria, pero no todos confían en que sea posible.

Durin e Ingór, príncipes de los Barbiluengos y de los Zhélruka, comandan a sus fuerzas conjuntamente para abrirse paso a través del hielo con el que Hrímil Corazónhelado selló las puertas de Gundabad. Una vez hayan entrado, el Gabil'akkâ comienza sus esfuerzos por hacerse con el control de la imponente corte de Máttugard.

Durin ha solicitado tu ayuda en la fortaleza de Skarháld en las Montañas Grises, donde busca unir a los clanes enanos allí reunidos: Hachetones, Zhélruka y Barbiluengos. Temiendo que su propio pueblo sea superado en número por otros clanes, ha enviado refuerzos desde la Montaña Solitaria: su padre el rey Thorin Yelmo de Piedra ha respondido dirigiendo un gran ejército de Barbiluengos, muchos de ellos veteranos de la distante Gran Guerra de los Orcos y la más reciente Batalla de los Cinco Ejércitos, para unirse a su hijo. Las tensiones se incrementan, pero no hacen que Durin cambie su objetivo de un premio valioso y difícil de ganar: Gundabad, el sagrado Hogar de la Montaña, actualmente en manos de los orcos.

Como paso previo al propósito de Durin de conquistar Gundabad, el hijo del rey Thorin Yelmo de Piedra ha enviado exploradores a los Manantiales del Langflood. Han vuelto con noticias de una partida de incursión orca enviada desde la fortaleza, y Durin te ha enviado antes de que maten a los habitantes de los Manantiales, o que frusten los planes para el asalto de su ejército al Hogar de la Montaña. Has eliminado el grupo de incursión orca, pero antes de que su líder muriera te habló de Gorgar el Despiadado, nuevo Señor de Gundabad, hijo de Bolg y hermano de Mazog, quien atribuló grandemente a los enanos en su intento de reconquistar Moria.

Formaciones naturales en los Manantiales del Langflood

The Floodfells are riddled with caves, but the Beornings who live in this area prefer not to explore their dark, narrow depths. Vile insects, pestilential bats, and burrowers with sharp teeth make their homes in these places, and the folk of Limlók only wish to concern themselves with these unpleasant creatures if they emerge into the sunlight or moonlight.
Explore the various natural curiosities to be found within the Wells of Langflood.
Explore the several natural curiosities to be found within the Wells of Langflood.

The rocky slopes of Veithhól serve as a den for the hunting-cats that stalk Misthallow. What few travellers find themselves in this area report the sound of soft, padding feet somewhere in the fog. The natural consequence of these reports seems obvious to the wiser among us: the cats must not have been hungry, or these reports would not exist.

The rocky pass of the Cabed Rhimdath serves as a path for those of the Holbytlan who dare to venture from the safety of their home in Lyndelby. For those few who have travelled into the Cabed Rhimdath, they have reported thick brambles and strange painted stones before turning around at the site of leering Eagles.

The narrow clefts of Scraper's Clough have been expanded by the tireless work of the cave-claws that live here, an industrious effort that is halted only when it is time for the creatures to feed. This they do on the hapless beasts that stumble into the Clough, and on adventurers who do the same. These latter meals tend to underestimate the creatures as \qmere cave-claws,\q a misjudgment the inhabitants of Scraper's Clough are only too pleased to encourage.

The great cascade of Reikfoss marks the location where the River Greylin flows out of the Elderslade into Misthallow to form one of the falls of the Three Sisters. Together, the vapours that rise from the base of Reikfoss and those of the Twainmantle blanket all of Misthallow in fog.

The two waterfalls of the Twainmantle are formed at the passage of the Langwell and a smaller stream out of Elderslade into Misthallow. Together with the Reikfoss, these three falls make up the Three Sisters, the combined vapour that rises from their bases enshrouding all of Misthallow in fog.

The question of these times, of great interest for Runerik Knotbeard and his people, not to mention the other folk who walk along the Wells of Langflood: are the Orcs and goblins who threaten these lands driven by the same hatreds and desires that have motivated them for hundreds of years, or is there a greater purpose that guides them to evil? It is a question that must be resolved, for it could mean the survival of those who live along the Langflood.

Settlements in the Wells of Langflood

After the death of their chieftain Bolg during the Battle of Five Armies, the Orcs of the Misty Mountains declined. This reduction in their numbers and their power would not last forever, but during this time the folk of Beorn were able to reassert their presence in the Floodfells, roaming the wilds more openly. In the Floodfells they built the village of Limlók, and it would be the most northern town of Beorn's folk.
Like the overgrown bushes and tangled roots in the low-lands, the Bear-folk are at their wildest in the Floodfells. Today the town's thane is Runerik Knotbeard, and he is distrustful of outsiders, believing his own people possess strength enough to turn away any chance raiding-parties from Gundabad or elsewhere.
Explore the various settlements to be found within the Wells of Langflood.
Explore the various settlements to be found within the Wells of Langflood.

Perhaps in years to come, when the history of the Éothéod has been expanded upon by Léothred's journey and his scholarly pursuits, the name Hlithseld will be held in high esteem. \qThis is where he camped on his journey for knowledge!\q folk may say... or they may not. It is not always easy to know what will be remembered.

The greatest threat posed by the wood-trolls of Grazadh-gropor is one of surprise, for the forested region that is their home creaks and sways with every breeze that troubles the settled fog. The sound of these tree-ish complaints serves to hide the approach of the wood-trolls until they are very near their victim, and then it is too late.

The Beornings of the Floodfells do not know if the wood-trolls of Shulgmokh are related to the Taurogrim of other lands, and do not much care. They are much more interested in how long it takes to tear out their vital heartwood, stopping their movements and the danger these creatures pose to Limlók.

The wargs of Ujâk-fulug would prefer to attack the weak and cowardly, but there are few enough of those in the Floodfells to begin with, for that land is hard and those who do live there are made tougher and stronger. The wargs content themselves with feasting upon beasts of the wild and goats who stray too far from their protectors, but these kills only sharpen their appetite for more challenging, filling meats.

This rustic hamlet of smials is nestled among steep cliffs, hidden until today from the eyes of the Wise and protected from discovery by the Eagle guardians who dwell atop the high peaks. Can this have been the last dwelling-place of the Holbytlan who once thrived in Misthallow and the Floodfells, and who often appeared in the folklore of the Éothéod? If so, it would be home to the descendants of those Fallohides who did not cross the Misty Mountains on their eventual road to what would become the Shire.

Thokvist has been Skarding Wolfsbane's home for many years, but the small yard is often untended; the Beorning spends most of his time hunting for hostile dangers among the foggy vales of Misthallow. When he does return home it is only for a short time, perhaps to enjoy one of the apples that grows on the trees outside his home and to rest briefly before setting out again.

Dúnabrygg crosses the river, allowing passage between Misthallow and the Floodfells. The stonework of the bridge has crumbled, but enterprising dwarves repaired the span with sturdy wooden construction.
Ruins in the Wells of Langflood
Find Dúnabrygg

The history of Sundergrót is shrouded in mystery, for it has been long-abandoned. Longbeard tradition holds that this great cleft overlooking the Floodfells was made by the impact of Durin's axe sometime during the First Age.
Today the ruins are haunted by goblins, but they know nothing of the ancient events that there took place. For the goblins it holds only the memory of dwarf-work, and that is a sharp dagger-point of hatred to them, though they covet the treasures and gems their foes unearth.
Explore the various ruins that dot the hills and valleys throughout the Wells of Langflood.
Explore the various ruined structures to be found within the Wells of Langflood.
Whoever Hengi may have been, and the knowledge of why this broken dwarf-bridge bears his name, has been lost to time.

The dwarf-bridge of Skerabrygg once permitted passage across the Langflood for those seeking to explore Sundergrót, but today the bridge is destroyed. Someone has hastily-repaired the span with planks of wood, but it seems a temporary solution. The weather and rain of the Floodfells will doubtless cast this path into the river before many days pass.
The goblins of Stramvárth root among the ruins of Sundergrót in search of treasure, fighting among themselves for the right to hold the most precious pieces.

The goblins and Orc-kind of Egvárth quarreled with their kindred to the east for the right to camp nearer to Sundergrót. It is a decision they may come to regret if more than treasures can be found in the depths of that cleft.

The great keep of the Ai-thúda was called Fasthálla, and it was the seat of their chief Frumgar. When it was burned and destroyed by Scatha the Worm, and Frumgar gravely wounded, his young son Fram swore vengeance upon the great wingless dragon. Eventually it was done, and Fram became Fram Wormsbane. The Ai-thúda rebuilt Fasthálla and gave it a new name: Framsburg.
From its location high atop a rocky spur in Misthallow, Framsburg could not be easily-conquered by Orcs, though they tested its defences and the resolve of its inhabitants from time to time. After the departure of the Éothéod, Framsburg gradually fell into ruin through neglect. It was never sacked, but in time it stood empty and Orcs prowled the ruin.
Today, worms and drakes have built nests among the skeletons of ancient buildings, and Framsburg is theirs. In this way perhaps Scatha has at last achieved his revenge upon Fram Wormsbane and the memory of his people.

The hill-trolls and their unpleasant allies have erected a barricade at Lumrog, watching passage along the road and allowing none to pass. Whether this obstruction is motivated by selfish gain or has been mandated by more cunning powers with greater designs is unknown.

At some time during the residency of the Éothéod in these lands, they carved the White Mare into a hillside in the Floodfells. Whether its distinctive shape was intended to represent the mearas they found grazing on the strip of land between the Twainmantles and the Reikfoss is not known, but seems likely. The White Mare is today faded and somewhat overgrown, but it remains a reminder of the Éothéod's love of horses.

Goblin Bounties of the Langflood
Many particularly troublesome goblins still lurk in the Wells of Langflood.

Among the most curious of the pursuits of the goblin called Earth-splitter was his fascination with the gems buried in the mountain-stones. This by itself was not unusual, for indeed most of goblin-kind coveted such shiny treasures, but Earth-splitter desired to find such gems for the purpose of eating them. Thanks to your efforts, Earth-splitter has eaten his last meal, and will no longer trouble the mines of dwarves. Others might well applaud you for this as well, for his literal appetite for gems was considered distasteful by others of his kind.

The Gangly Slicer made his home among the cave-claws of Scraper's Clough. It was an uneasy alliance, and did not happen overnight; it took one horn-gouged goblin and several sliced cave-claws before these opponents learned to live in peace. Once they did, they each united in their hatred of those foolish enough to brave the Clough. That the Gangly Slicer was once one of these was left unspoken among the cave-claws, or so we must assume.

'Goblins do not like to come aboveground unless they must, so I do not know if this Forest-stalker is real. If he is, he may be desperate, and that will make him more dangerous. But perhaps you are more dangerous than he?' - Runerik Knotbeard

'Bear-cleaver? It is just a name. I do not believe this goblin has slain a single one of my people, or any of the bears that live in the Wells. Not by himself, at any rate! I will slay him myself for taking such a name, if you do not get to him first.' - Runerik Knotbeard

'You can hear Drudge-stomper coming from very far away, for he has unusually heavy footfalls for a goblin. It makes avoiding him quite easy, which is for the best, for I hear he is quite deadly with his weapon.' - Yrsa Spearwife
'Pine not for Pine-cleaver.' - Anonymous
'What does his name mean? What do you think it means? It means he cooks his meals in the skulls of his enemies! I'd have thought that was obvious.' - Yrsa Spearwife

The goblin called Blood-spiller has done his share of that during the weeks he has stalked the Wells of Langflood. Thanks to your efforts, not a drop more will he spill, and the lands along the river will be made safer.

The Wound-skewer is no more. This goblin preferred to leave his victims alive but bleeding, and delighted to follow them from a safe distance until they finally succumbed to other predators in the wild. Thanks to your efforts, this distasteful practice is now ended, as is the Wound-skewer himself.

None know what so-infuriated the Angry Chaser, and that makes the sound of him approaching all the more frightening. Thanks to your efforts, his anger and his chasing have both been quelled, and the folk in the Wells need fear his approach no longer.

'There are no bees in the dark places of the world, for they desire the sweet taste of nectar, and sunlight, and warm breezes, and those can only be found aboveground. But they are not the only creature with a sting, and if you are not careful, some among the goblins may have a deadlier sting than any you have felt before.' - Yrsa Spearwife

'He will smell you out well before you know he tracks you, and with knives and daggers he has skill unparalleled. The Tracking Dagger has slain none of my folk, but he has given a fright to more than one, and it is only their keen senses that have spared them.' - Yrsa Spearwife

Goblins prefer to remain underground, wrapped in the safety of their darkness, but when need drives them to hunt in daylight they are emboldened and made more dangerous. So it was with Marsh-reaver, who stalked the fens and forests of the Wells of Langflood. Harried by the Great Eagles who watched the hidden pass to Lyndelby, Marsh-reaver never found his way to the home of the Holbytlan. Thanks to your efforts, now he never will.

Raging Mauler was a goblin of few words, and those he did speak consisted entirely of threats and insults. More than a few of his kind suffered injuries at his hands, for his was a careless ire. His short tale is now ended, thanks to your efforts, and none even among the goblins will mourn his passing.

Crag-slaver was the brother of the goblin called Blade-slaver, and while folk spoke in hushed tones of his infamous sibling, Crag-slaver rarely merited a mention. He will no longer threaten the folk of the Wells from the blanket of anonymity that enveloped him.
'I wonder what ever became of Blade-slaver?' curious children will ask. 'He was an only child,' the bards will reply. 'Let us be glad he had no siblings!'

Blade-slaver, one of the goblins that haunted the Wells of Langflood, is no more. Among goblins he had a reputation for cruelty matched only by his brother Crag-slaver. Thanks to your efforts he will no longer add to that fell reputation.

The Death-spear moved in darkness, but slowly. He preferred to remain immobile, hiding in pools of shadow deep within the caves that were his favourite haunts. Thanks to your efforts, he will no longer leap out upon unsuspecting victims.

'The goblin called Shadow-ripper is so stealthy he lives among the great cats of Veithhól, and they do not know they share their den with one such as he! It's true! Why, if he were to die there, I think he could go unnoticed by them even in death!' - Trygvar, son of Runerik
'The secret to escaping the Beast Master is to show no fear. Only then might you escape. The secret to killing him? Ah, I know of no such secret. Have you learned of such a way?' - Runerik Knotbeard

The Goblins of the Wells rely upon the weak and unsuspecting for their meals, but there is fewer such prey with each passing day. The goblin called Bone-chewer took his name for his ability to make one such kill last for as much as a week, and he was revered by others of his kind for his ability to ration such a meal for so long. Now that he is slain, one wonders if his own bones will be used to flavour a long-lasting soup for the others of his kind, and what he would think of such a happenstance?
Many particularly troublesome goblins still lurk in the Wells of Langflood.

The question of these times, of great interest for Runerik Knotbeard and his people, not to mention the other folk who walk along the Wells of Langflood: are the Orcs and goblins who threaten these lands driven by the same hatreds and desires that have motivated them for hundreds of years, or is there a greater purpose that guides them to evil? It is a question that must be resolved, for it could mean the survival of those who live along the Langflood.

Despite the many long years it has endured, Annâk-khurfu continues to stand tall. The dwarves have rallied to these ruins and called their allies to arms, preparing for the inevitable.
Annâk-khurfu offers an advantageous view of the main roads leading into Elderslade -- from Ered Mithrin to the east, and Misthallow to the south -- where friend and foe can be spotted plainly.

The years have not been kind to Zarkul-sulûn, which now plays host to all manner of evil: Orcs, hobgoblins, wargs, and perhaps others.
The ruins sit too closely to Annâk-khurfu for the dwarves' comfort. They keep a wary eye on Zarkul-sulûn, understanding that it will be the first of many obstacles they must cross if they wish to retake Gundabad.
The forces of Gundabad have long held Shakal-atrâd within their grasp. Though all appears quiet outside these foreboding ruins, delving deeper may reveal otherwise....
Zudramdân may not be as formidable as Annâk-khurfu, but the dwarves' northern camp allows them some modicum of safety in the long fight to retake their home.

The rushing waterfalls of the Greylin River drown out even the loudest of sounds at Grálinvarth. From this vantage point, one can easily spot the Rushgate and Annâk-khurfu, as well as glimpse the valley of Misthallow on a clear day.

Crude constructions deface the Gates of Gundabad, a mocking reminder of the dwarves' losses and defeats. One might wonder what else the Orcs have done to further corrupt the former dwarf-kingdom past this foreboding threshold.

Perched above the Greylin River, the Hárveg Bridge had been, until recently, broken and impassable. The dwarves have skilfully mended the bridge, opening safe passage to and from Misthallow once more.
