Corsairs have taken up residence here at Khataj Mârsa, giving them easy access to the islands that make up Bakhjâd to the north-west and the large island of Zamarzîr to the south-east.

The pestilential creatures known as kergrim are drawn to death and the dying, and there have been both at this site of wrecks and ruins. Many sailors have fallen into the sailor's grave that is Bâkhabar.

This island is home to a species of beetle that scurries all over the rocks north of Jeb Khâtel. Few locations throughout Zîrar Tarka have been named as appropriately as Ghax-hophra, which means 'living burrow' in the Umbari language.

The sound of the ferocious drakes that crawl upon Jeb Lipha carries a great distance over the water, warning those who travel in Zîrar Tarka not to approach this place, which means 'serpent-stone' in the Umbari language.

Dor Pherkha, the 'cat's cleft,' is located on the southern side of Jeb Khâtel. It may be partially responsible for the island's reputation, for anyone who draws too near the creatures living here are likely to become their prey, and tonight's meal can bring no tales forth from the island.

Maj Khibi, the 'netted grove,' is home to a particularly unpleasant breed of spider. It is said that in years past this place had other denizens, but once the spiders decided to move in none desired to stay for long.

Corsairs camp beside the lagoon decorated with the shipwrecks torn apart by the Grinding Jaws of Shedax Khîn. Is it because the broken hulls remind them of nature's cruelty or the whims of the Valar? Or is it because the newly-created wrecks may provide easy pickings for seekers of treasure? None can say for certain.

Bax Garâkh, the 'drowning shallows,' are located to the east of Bakhjâd. Despite the possibility of finding valuable treasure among the wrecks torn apart by Shedax Khîn, few dare to trespass. It is said the Dead guard that treasure, and only the very foolish or the very fortunate would risk their wrath.

Ghar Jâdam, the 'grotto of bones,' is located on Zamarzîr, the largest island of the chain that makes up Zîrar Tarka. It is home to jungle-beasts of great size and strength, and the wiser residents of Halrax have learned to give the creatures a wide berth. The less wise among them have gone on to decorate the grotto themselves.

Basha Ghând, the 'hungry bog,' is located on the northern side of Bakhjâd. Corsairs of Mâr Naphra have disappeared in this area during recent weeks, but whether they ran afoul of natural hazards or some type of beast is currently unknown.

Dar Grekhûl, the 'lizard-home,' can be found on the eastern side of Zamarzîr. The legs of the salamanders that live here are said to be a culinary delicacy, if you can discover the correct means of preparing them. Any of the residents of Halrax who know the secret, however, are not inclined to share it.

Baj Khatûg, the 'slashing shore,' is a wide beach on the south-eastern island of Zîrar Tarka, nearest to the Cape of Umbar. It is home to large crabs that both pinch and scuttle. Rumour has it their meat is delicious, if you can avoid the pinching and overcome the scuttling.

You have discovered Voyage's End

The waters that surround Zîrar Tarka are treacherous for the unprepared, but even skilled mariners can stray too near the isles when storms arise in the Bay of Belfalas, to their deep sorrow. If they have the luck of the Valar, some of their crew survive to see the dawning sun that peeks through the forest canopy at Voyage's End. If they do not only the shattered hulks remain, standing in the water beside the island chain, decorating the smile of Shedax Khîn, the Grinding Jaws, from that day forward.

The sizeable settlement of Halrax is located on Zamarzîr, the largest of the isles that make up the chain of Zîrar Tarka. It was built over a period of many years by the freebooters of the Bay of Belfalas, and although most of its residents come and go every few years, in this they remain consistent: they prize their freedom and individuality above all else, and answer to none but themselves. Halrax has become a place for the lost, where those who have nowhere else to go sometimes find themselves, through no plan of their own.

Residents elsewhere in Zîrar Tarka believe the northern island of Jeb Khâtel to be uninhabited, and the Orkish voices that carry from the high cliffs of that place do little to encourage their visitation. But Kafagur has become the new home of a number of unexpected travellers, far from their ancestral lands.

'Listen well to me, friend,' Manadhon says carefully, filling a mug almost to the top with ale. The bartender of Halrax keeps his eyes trained on you, but his pour is so well-practised that not a drop is spilled.
'No one goes that far to the north. Do you know why?'
You shake your head.
'In the Umbari language, Phadâl Bimai... it means \qWreckage of the Brutes.\q You are better off staying here, believe me. It has a dangerous reputation.'

'Where did you hear that name?' Manadhon asks, and you say you heard someone mention it in passing. The bartender of Halrax thinks for a moment.
'I have never climbed up to it myself, but I have felt the chill in my bones when the one who lives there has flown over the town, the shadow of her vast wings falling upon me. I think it is an ill omen, friend, and you would be wise to forget the name Aklâradum. She lives there, and as long as she stays home we can live in peace. At least... that is what I have always believed.'

'You cannot spend long on the island of Zamarzîr without noticing the great caldera beside our town,' Manadhon muses at sunset one night. 'It was not always a lake, you know. They say it used to be a volcano... let us hope it remains dormant. That name, though... sometimes I wonder if the name speaks true.'
You ask Manadhon the name of which he speaks, and he looks you in the eye.
'Irkhadâr,' he says. 'In the Umbari language it means \qThe Sleeper.\q'

Grijâti, the Home of the Stranded, lies on the western shore of the Cape of Umbar. Haradrim remain here, hoping to usurp control from the Kindred of the Coins.
Súlstron, the Raider's Refuge, led by the goblin Corsair Shakfut Slit-throat, is a makeshift encampment at the foot of the mountains of the Cape of Umbar.

Kâshtabil, the Crawling Tangle, is a burbling swamp filled with driftwood, crabs, and nerbyg. The filthy waters are the source of many ills that plague the nearby village of Khûtra.

In the shadow of The Mâkhda Korbo lies Gherja Mût, the Barrens of the Dead. The risen dead creeping through these ruins are a mix of ancient and the freshly dead creatures reanimated by Sauron's lingering power.

Pirates loyal to neither the fallen Heirs of Castamir nor the reigning Kindred of the Coins attack ships on the sea north of the Cape of Umbar and bring their spoils ashore to Bêkhmol, the Free Wharf.
Jâghimsa, the Wandering Wood, is home to huorns and a fearsome wood-troll herder and lies on the hillside to the north and east of Rakhatâb.
The Grim Shelter, or Kan Skûrja, is the makeshift home of the nomadic Corsairs who still raid the seas along the Shield Isles and Cape of Umbar.

Ghadir Sûd, the Black Pools, speaks to ancient wellsprings of tar that bubbled up on the land long ago. These bubbling dark springs drew the salamanders that still dwell there today. Though the wellsprings are gone, the salamanders remain.

Hâtaphor, the Snatcher's Den, is a dangerous area east of Umbar Baharbêl home to a particularly dangerous brood of spiders. The same brood's silk is prized by tailors in the city and often workers are snatched while attempting to recover the silken webbings in the den.
Travellers finding themselves in Bâlakhat, the Devourer's Waters, often do not return. The fearsome crocodiles making this area their home are known for their penchant for flesh.
Idwadâr, the Writhen-home, in the foothills outside of Umbar Baharbêl is home to the rock worms of Umbar. These beasts protect their nest with great ferocity and are a natural enemy of the people.

Bog-lurkers covered in reeds make Taj-kâta, the Mire-flats, their ancestral home. Here, the creatures lived in peace for centuries. Now, hunters scour the Mire-flats to acquire seeds and legs from the bog-lurkers to supply the cooks of Umbar Baharbêl.

Jêbel Lakha, the Gathering-stone, is home to two warring prides of lions led by the brothers Skûr and Kabûro. Both beasts have long attacked foolish explorers who wander too close to the territory. The brothers stalk the savannah and stones of Jêbel Lakha in pursuit of one another.

Khûtra is a fishing village on the bay in the Cape of Umbar. The village is recently plagued by an illness claiming livestock and men. The villagers seek a cure for this malady so they can return to their normal lives.
Jid Phêsi is the Cavern of Whispers, located in the hills north of Rakhatâb. Miners venture into the depths in search of rich ore, gems, and other riches to fuel the industry of the outpost.

Rakhatâb is the largest settlement on the Cape of Umbar. Here, workers toil day and night to keep the forge fires burning for the Kindred of the Coins. The fall of the Heirs of Castamir gave hope to the workers, but the transition to the Kindred of the Coins' leadership is fraught with difficulties.

Deeds of Umbar Baharbêl

In the aftermath of the Sea-stone Mutiny, Umbar Baharbêl has been freed from the Heirs of Castamir and their rulers in the Empire of Ordâkh. Under the governance of the Kindred of the Coins, a council of seven chosen by the citizens of Umbar Baharbêl, the City of the Corsairs struggles to be reborn as a Free City—with tidings of hope and treachery found in equal measure as its people step out from the darkness that was cast upon them long ago by the Dark Lord, Sauron.

You have discovered Calatirion, the Beacon-tower, which was raised by King Elendil to celebrate his victory over Sauron. However, the tower would not stand forever, for the Dark Lord's servants were not gone, and they would return in a later age. At the command of the Forsaken Reaver, one of the Nazgûl, the Calatirion was toppled. The day of its downfall came to be called the Death of Light, and the horror of it is remembered still by the oldest residents of the city.

You have discovered Bor Sêma, Tower of the Sky, the ruined observatory that stands on a hill above the city. Once a haven for those who studied the stars and sought to find meaning in the night sky, it was destroyed by the Church of the All-seeing and the servants of Sauron.

Explore the Sail-haven, the Upper Ward, the Tor-gardens, the Lower Ward, the Fleet-fast, and the Shoreward Stone in Umbar Baharbêl, the City of the Corsairs.
You have discovered the Barracks, where soldiers of the Fleet-fast are outfitted with armour and weapons for their guard duty and given their assignments.
You have discovered the Baths of Ishkun, where soldiers of the Fleet-fast are permitted to wash the grime from their clothes after their shifts.
You have discovered the Soldiers' Mess-hall, where guards on duty in the Fleet-fast take their meals.
You have discovered the Baths of Kadax, where citizens of the Lower Ward are encouraged to find a respite from the grime and dust of the city.

You have discovered the Fathomwell, a deep and wide pool that collects sea-water that can then be put to use by residents of the city or for fighting fires. Two fishermen come to the Fathomwell every day, and have done so without fail since they were children.

You have discovered the Gut, a warren of narrow streets and alleys that is not especially safe for outsiders to dare unless they keep a careful watch upon their belongings. Residents of the Gut are a hardy sort, and suspicious of outsiders or folk from the wealthier regions of the city. The Sea-stone Mutiny began in the Gut and areas nearby.

Eshmun, the Captain of the Haven, keeps a careful watch upon the goings-on throughout the Sail-haven from his post at the Harbour-warden's Tower. He is a loyal ally of the Kindred of the Coins and eagerly awaits the return of Tumúldo Fierce-water, who he expects to sail back to Umbar any day now.

You have discovered the Fleet-fast Gaol, where those who are found guilty of committing crimes are held until it is determined what should be done with them. Many of these folk choose trial-by-combat in the arena as a means of earning their freedom, hoping beyond hope that they are not matched up against Rothog the Storm when their number is drawn.

You have discovered the Fleet-fast Parade Ground, where soldiers march before the assembled leaders of the Kindred of the Coins. Such gatherings have not been common of late, but in time of peace, when ceremony is required, the Parade Grounds will be ready.

You have discovered the Stûna, where ships of the Corsairs dock. Most of the fleet was lost at Pelargir during the War of the Ring, but some ships remain, now under the command of the Kindred of the Coins.

In the Umbari tongue, the locations where stand the great bones of ships under construction are called Jâsh-bithi. This is the southernmost of the two largest, and it is overseen by Râmax, who has sworn to see the Heirsworn who remain in the Sail-haven defeated at last.

You have discovered Dâr Irkant, the auction house of Umbar, through which a great deal of currency flows both into and from the coffers of the Upper Ward's merchant families. Hármelak, the Golden Queen, keeps a careful eye upon the business conducted at Dâr Irkant.
You have discovered the Baths of Ilmai Iforikh, known to local residents as the Flowering Waters. The peaceful tranquility of these baths are reputed to soothe both body and mind.
You have discovered Dâr Rapha, the House of Tales, a great amphitheatre constructed by the Númenóreans. It frequently plays host to Umbari singers and storytellers.
You have discovered the Wharf-beacon, which welcomes ships arriving to the Sail-haven from long voyages away at sea, guiding them to safety when they arrive at night.

In the Umbari tongue, the locations where stand the great bones of ships under construction are called Jâsh-bithi. This is the northernmost of the two largest, and it is overseen by Ahûd, who has worked among the ships of the Sail-haven for many years.

You have discovered Dâr Jeraf, the grand academy of the Tor-gardens that was once known as the House of Wisdom. It was destroyed by servants of the Church of the All-Seeing, and now only rubble remains as a reminder of the damage done by the followers of Sauron.

You have discovered Kamîr Kateb. the scriptorium that once held countless records and histories of Umbar Baharbêl. Now it has fallen into disrepair and disuse, and the Chambers of Records gather only dust.

You have discovered Dâr Tabib, the partially-ruined apothecary that was known at one time as the House of Healers. Like other structures of learning and knowledge in the Tor-gardens, the Church of the All-seeing exacted a cruel toll upon Dâr Tabib.

You have discovered Dahâl Huliz, the grand gladiatorial arena of Umbar Baharbêl. Much blood has been spilt in the arena during many years of the city's history, and on the night of the Sea-stone Mutiny, even more was spilled when Rothog the Storm turned his gaze upon the Heirs of Castamir spectating in the stands.

You have discovered Bith Gabâr, the grand forum and meeting-place of the Upper Ward. It retains an air of enduring permanence granted to it by the presence of abundant Númenórean architecture, and has been known to draw folk of all sorts who wish to draw attention to themselves or their activities.

You have discovered Dâr Laja, the Meeting-hall, located at the head of the great forum in the Upper Ward. This hall is one of the remaining intact Númenórean structures in the city, and is the location where the Kindred of the Coins often convene for official business.

You have proven yourself by scouring the Isle of Storms, braving the Streets of Râhal Bakh, enchanting the crowd in the arena of Dahâl Huliz, and surviving the Depths of the Mâkhda Khorbo. None can question your tenacity and determination, and by completing all these deeds, you have earned great favour throughout Umbar Baharbêl.
Khâshap makes for the Sea Shadow to deliver a vile substance from Thaurisgar. Your pursuit has brought you to the Streets of Râhal Bakh.
The lords of Umbar have requested that you find the nesting place of this monstrous bird and drive it from the Shield Isles.
The gladiatorial pits of Umbar Baharbêl serve several important purposes: entertaining the masses, keeping their attention focused, and meting justice upon those who break the laws of the city.

After the confrontation in the Citadel of Winds, the ship bearing Azagath, Belondor, and Nakási, Reaper of the Waves sails north-west into the shadow cast by the Mâkhda Khorbo. Pursuing the trio, you enter the depths of a long-hidden cavern leading through dank, twisting passages ending at an iron-wrought gate. The smells of the sea, iron, and ash assail you as you press deeper beneath the land and closer to the remnants of the temple ruins.

Ishadôkh lies within the southern reaches of Tâkhdar, but the hissing and buzzing sounds emanating from the workers and burrowers of this hive travel much further than you might expect. Refugees in Kamrabezûr have complained about the sound from even as far away as the chamber beneath Dahâl Huliz.
The smugglers of Sâl Bajat keep a wary eye upon the nearby market, eager to arrange as many favourable \qdeals\q for themselves and their customers as they can.

The spiders of Shak Phêlex are a venomous danger for any who stumble down the wrong passage within Tâkhdar. Folk in the city above keep some crates here, but the presence of the spiders may have persuaded some of these merchants to count these goods a loss.

The cross-roads of Tilmakhím, not far from the centre of Tâkhdar, have become home to two types of Umbar-môkh resident. The first are vendors seeking to stand out from their fellows at other markets beneath the city. The second are the rats, drawn by the crowds and the promise of food scraps. Each demands attention from you, and will not be silenced without effort.

Deshûkh is closed to outsiders, but the criminal element is alive and well in this area of Dil-irmíz. Smugglers, cutthroats, and pickpockets coexist in these chambers, but only for so long as their chosen occupations do not hinder those of their fellows.

The name Dâr Sêkhta has been spoken of in hushed tones for the past few weeks, with the whispered rumours hinting that a new power has begun to rise in the damp passages and sealed chambers of Dil-irmíz. Does someone seek to challenge Khôltekh for dominance in the Berths?

The tombs of Lôkhalel have seized the attention of raiders seeking to plunder the crypts for treasure and priceless trinkets. From here the particularly bold sometimes strike out for the adjoining passages of Khabârkhad, endangering anyone they see as competition for the valuables within.

Nishabêt, \qweavers' nest\q in the Umbari tongue, used to refer to one small chamber within Khabârkhad. Without enough guards to stem the tide of spiders as they emerged, the nest has expanded and now occupies the encircling passages. Unless something is done, Nishabêt may one day become the name for all of Umbar-môkh.

A vaulted, distant ceiling and wide avenues mark the tombs where the nobility of Umbar Baharbêl were once given their eternal rest, but the silent sepulcher of Sektakhâb is no longer peaceful. Now the restless Dead stalk these crypts in south-west Khabârkhad, endangering any who risk coming near.

If these halls were ever a place of safety, they are no longer, for the Ugikh-hûti now threaten any who pass this way, naming their foothold here Jâx Ugikh. Between escaped beasts from the arena and this group of hostile cultists, the wide passages of Kamrabezûr are no longer suitable for the scholars from the Tor-gardens who seek solace within the cool passages beneath the city.

These corridors are far from the crypts and tombs of Khabârkhad, but the Dead walk in Kamrabezûr even so. It would take a learned scholar to understand what has disturbed their rest and caused them to shamble here, but few such learned ones would dare approach Ghâr Mejet.

The warriors of Harkhaphâr fight without mercy, as if they remain upon the bloodstained sands of Dahâl Huliz. Can they still hear the distant roar of the crowd from the stands above, or are they merely the echoes of their past adulation? Blinded by rage and the ferocity of the combats they imagine continue, they speak no word in answer.

In the Umbari tongue, Hulzidâr means \qhome of the fighters,\q and in the days of unrest following the withdrawal of the Empire of Ordakh from the city, it has become a most suitable name. Former warriors of the Dahâl Huliz defend the outskirts of the camp and make safe the other refugees that now shelter in the chambers beneath the arena.

The crocodiles of Ilmabiri gather around the water that plunges into Nêb-jadir. Long ago they learned that any creatures that endured the drop will not long survive their jaws, and the lesson applies equally to two-legged adventurers as it does to four-legged beasts.
Something haunts the small encampment of Talaba-kên, but whether these structures are home to displaced children of Umbar or something else is a question of some interest to those who guard Ilmabiri.

Môba Ided has become home to a number of folk who have few other places to turn. Both fleeing Heirsworn and cultists from the Church of the All-Seeing have taken up residence in the southern reaches of Ilmabiri, achieving a delicate peace among themselves. That temporary understanding does not extend to outsiders.

Derrota al Sureño Sombrío
¡Has participado en la derrota del Sureño Sombrío!

Los Nueve han sido liberados en la Tierra Media para perseguir a todos aquellos que se opongan a la voluntad de Sauron. Los héroes de la Tierra Media deben unirse y devolver a las sombras a estos infames lugartenientes del Señor Oscuro.
Derrota al Sureño Sombrío

Pocos entre los vivos lo escucharon hablar, pero su rostro era bien conocido y temido. Lo llamaban el Sureño Sombrío, y mientras los Hombres temblaban ante su presencia durante la Segunda Edad, durante la Tercera la leyenda de su malicia solo había crecido. En días posteriores, fue él a quien Lhaereth la Manchada siguió en secreto a Dol Guldur, donde descubrió a Sauron y lo ayudó a recuperarse, por un precio. ¿El Señor Oscuro recompensó o castigó la falta de su Nazgûl? Pero eso fue mucho más tarde. Durante la Segunda Edad, el Sureño Sombrío era conocido solo por ser paciente, leal y silencioso.
Derrota a la Amargura de Khand
¡Has derrocado a la Amargura de Khand!

Los Nueve han sido liberados en la Tierra Media para cazar a todos aquellos que se opongan a la voluntad de Sauron. Los héroes de la Tierra Media deben unirse y devolver a las sombras a estos infames lugartenientes del Señor Oscuro.
Derrota a la Amargura de Khand

Era la Amargura de Khand y, con la bendición de Sauron, avanzó por las tierras no conquistadas y las reclamó para el Señor Oscuro. El anillo que se le otorgó se llamaba Adâsh, y muchos fueron los enemigos que creó, muchos los orgullosos guerreros que abatió. Encontraba gran alegría en provocar la guerra, y siempre lo había hecho, pero con el poder otorgado por Sauron, la Amargura de Khand se volvió cada vez más mortal, más implacable y más despiadada.
Derrota al Rey Brujo
¡Has derrocado al Rey Brujo!

Los Nueve han sido liberados en la Tierra Media para cazar a todos aquellos que se opongan a la voluntad de Sauron. Los héroes de la Tierra Media deben unirse y devolver a las sombras a estos infames lugartenientes del Señor Oscuro.
Derrota al Rey Brujo

El más grande y temido de los Nueve, el Rey Brujo acechaba el campo de batalla pero rara vez, dejando las fortalezas de Mordor solo bajo la orden más urgente de Sauron. En años posteriores, el Señor de los Nazgûl levantaría de la nada la Tierra de Angmar, utilizándola para avanzar en el objetivo del Señor Oscuro de destruir el reino del norte de Arnor, pero al final de la Segunda Edad eso aún estaba lejos en las brumas del Tiempo. Durante el Asedio de Barad-dûr, el Rey Brujo se encontraba probando las debilidades de los ejércitos alineados contra su maestro, buscando el premio más valioso de todos: la información.
Derrota al Despojador Proscrito
¡Has derrocado al Despojador Proscrito!

Los Nueve han sido liberados en la Tierra Media para cazar a todos aquellos que se opongan a la voluntad de Sauron. Los héroes de la Tierra Media deben unirse y devolver a las sombras a estos infames lugartenientes del Señor Oscuro.
Derrota al Despojador Proscrito

Desde el lejano sur llegó, trayendo miedo y fuego a cada costa que espiaba con su cristal. Su reinado era de sangre, y la extraía de todos los que vivían a la vista y al olor del Mar. ¿Fue esa la razón por la que Sauron le dio el anillo Khânto, que es el Dador de Dolor? Con el poder de él, el Despojador Proscrito no podía ser detenido, y su risa se extendía tierra adentro con vientos funestos; estaba entre los sirvientes más rápidos y crueles de Sauron.
Derrota a la Espada Negra de Lebennin

Los Nueve han sido liberados en la Tierra Media para cazar a todos aquellos que se opongan a la voluntad de Sauron. Los héroes de la Tierra Media deben unirse y devolver a las sombras a estos infames lugartenientes del Señor Oscuro.
Derrota a la Espada Negra de Lebennin

En días posteriores, la Espada Negra de Lebennin fue vista con frecuencia merodeando entre las colinas y los bosques de Gondor Occidental, infundiendo miedo en los corazones de los Hombres con su temible presencia y su espada mortal. Para aquellos pocos que no huían, sus palabras caían como miel en sus oídos reacios y los llevaban a cometer terribles actos de maldad. Esto pudo haber demostrado ser su peor y más eficaz arma.
Derrota al Sumo Hechicero de Harad
¡Has derrocado al Sumo Hechicero de Harad!

Los Nueve han sido liberados en la Tierra Media para cazar a todos aquellos que se opongan a la voluntad de Sauron. Los héroes de la Tierra Media deben unirse y devolver a las sombras a estos infames lugartenientes del Señor Oscuro.
Derrota al Sumo Hechicero de Harad

Lo llamaban el Sumo Hechicero de Harad, pero para la mayoría de los que luchaban contra Sauron era solo un nombre. Rara vez salía de los calabozos de Mordor, ya que se deleitaba en la realización de rituales abominables y en el dominio de la magia oscura, y dedicaba su pensamiento a poco más. Pero cuando el Señor Oscuro consideraba oportuno enviarlo, Hombres y Elfos sabían que debían darle un amplio margen, o sufrir. Era Mêbat quien llevaba, el Devorador de Alegría, y dondequiera que iba, había un fin a la risa, y solo el inicio del dolor.
Derrota a la Languidez de Nurn
¡Has derrocado a la Languidez de Nurn!

Derrota a la Languidez de Nurn

Nadie puede decir qué barco lo llevó a la Tierra Media antes de que Númenor se perdiera, pero una vez que aceptó el regalo de Sauron, ya no podía ser contado entre los Hombres de esa tierra. Habitó en Thaurband, una fortaleza en el sur de Mordor, no lejos del Mar Interior. Desde esa fortaleza se extendió el miedo hacia él, dándole un nuevo título para reemplazar el nombre que ya no necesitaba. Se convirtió en la Languidez de Núrn, aunque no permaneció allí, y vagó por todas partes bajo el mando de Sauron.

¡Has derrocado al Jinete Maldito!

Los Nueve han sido liberados en la Tierra Media para cazar a todos aquellos que se opongan a la voluntad de Sauron. Los héroes de la Tierra Media deben unirse y devolver a las sombras a estos infames lugartenientes del Señor Oscuro.
Derrota al Jinete Maldito

Se movía rápidamente por el campo de batalla, persiguiendo a los guerreros que se atrevían a enfrentarse a él, cada vez menos a medida que avanzaba el asedio. Era el Jinete Maldito, y el sonido de su acercamiento convertía incluso la sangre más valiente en agua. En años posteriores comandaría ejércitos desde dentro de los muros de Dol Guldur, pero durante la Segunda Edad prefería luchar desde el lomo de su corcel negro, solo.

Derrota al Daño de Rhûn

Una vez fue un gran rey en tierras lejanas al este, acostumbrado a gobernar y reacio a inclinar la rodilla ante cualquier otro. Pero luego vino un dador de regalos y un prometedor de poder, y al aceptar estos señuelos, el gran rey cambió. Ya no gobernaba sus tierras con misericordia, y tampoco permanecía en su propio reino. Se convirtió en el Daño de Rhûn, y con ese nombre llegó a ser conocido como el Daño de Rhûn, y en otros lugares.

A medida que los Ordâkhai pierden el control de Ambarûl, la falta de ley va en aumento. Asesinos y maleantes, muchos de ellos desertores de los Ordâkhai, se han agrupado en un campamento en Bidrokh-nûn, desde el cual atacan a los habitantes del lugar y a las caravanas comerciales que pasan por la carretera cercana.
En el sitio de una ruina de origen desconocido, los servales y caracales de Ambarûl han hecho un hogar cómodo para sí mismos.
En lo profundo de los pantanos de Ambarûl, Gurakhu es el lugar de anidación de los zizani, las criaturas conocidas en otras partes de la Tierra Media como Niquebriques.
Las arenas secas de Nirikal, en el sur de Ambarûl, proporcionan el hábitat perfecto para los usan-kûni, los escorpiones gigantes de Shagâna.
Las colinas de Tûl Ushu, en el noreste de Ambarûl, son el hogar de muchos usan-kûni, los escorpiones gigantes de Shagâna.
Shegdush, que significa \qhogar de cerdos\q en shagâni, es el terreno de juego favorito de los jabalíes del este de Ambarûl.
En los pantanos de las orillas del sur del Ikorbân, los mosquitos se reúnen en Umûn Khab.

Antiguamente el principal pueblo pesquero de Ambarûl, Eshadûr ha caído bajo la ocupación de los Ordâkhai. Tras ser derrotadas por Girhâzi y la revuelta Ambarûli, la mayoría de las fuerzas Ordâkhai huyeron al sur del Ikorbân, expulsaron a los antiguos habitantes de Eshadûr y establecieron allí su nueva base de operaciones. Desde aquí ponen a prueba las defensas Dumûri y esperan refuerzos del sur para recuperar el control de Iridír y el norte de Ambarûl.

Los soldados de Ordâkhai han establecido un campamento en Khetsok, en la orilla sur del río Ikorbân. Desde aquí, disputan a los Dumûri el control del paso del río Vado de Algas y regulan el acceso a Ambarûl desde el sur.

Explora los campamentos, asentamientos y guaridas enemigas en Ambarûl, en el valle del Ikorbân.

Los soldados del Gran Imperio del Sur de Ordâkh que sobrevivieron a la revuelta de Ambarûl se han reagruparon en Omboha. Incapaces de llegar a sus compatriotas al sur del Ikorbân, reúnen sus fuerzas mientras esperan un rescate poco probable.

Encuentra a Iridír

Una serie de balsas unidas entre sí forman el Vado de Algas, el único paso de río actualmente en Ambarûl. El puente improvisado se construyó tras la destrucción del Puente de la Inundación hace unos cien años, y es actualmente el principal objeto de conflicto entre los Dumûri y los Ordâkhai restantes en Ambarûl.

Mehêtur es una granja de papiro en funcionamiento. El papiro, la planta, se cultiva aquí y luego se procesa en papiro, la superficie de escritura. Sin la presencia de los Ordâkhai, hay poca demanda de papiro en Ambarûl, ya que la población agraria es en gran parte analfabeta.

Ekagar es una granja de arroz en funcionamiento en la orilla norte del Ikorbân. El arroz es un cultivo ideal para los pantanos de Ambarûl y es un alimento básico de la dieta local. También es un excelente producto comercial, ya que puede secarse, lo que facilita su almacenamiento y transporte.
Un pequeño campamento de leñadores recién fundado, Gishtir se estableció con la esperanza de cosechar los árboles con madera de mayor calidad en un bosque cercano.

Un bosquecillo de árboles antiguos difícil de encontrar cerca del borde norte de Ambarûl, Arwáth fue durante mucho tiempo rumoreado como embrujado. En realidad, es un oasis habitado por los Elfos Kinta, actualmente ocupado solo por un guardián y los espíritus de los Kintai que se desvanecieron allí.

Cuando el Imperio de Ordâkh prohibió la alfabetización para los nativos de Ambarûl, los seguidores de las Viejas Vías se apresuraron a recopilar todos los pergaminos y libros relacionados con la historia y la cultura de Ambarûl para salvarlos de la destrucción. Esta colección de documentos fue escondida para su preservación, y la ubicación de donde se almacena ha sido olvidada durante mucho tiempo.

Este templo de Barkhûsh, un templo de Sauron, el que todo lo ve, no es más que una cáscara quemada después de la revuelta de Ambarûl, liderada por Girhâzi, lo destruyó hace meses. Fue una vez el hogar de los sacerdotes de Sauron, quienes sometían a la población local a la voluntad de su Señor. Casi inmediatamente después de enterarse de la derrota tanto del Señor Oscuro como del Emperador de Ordâkh, los campesinos de Ambarûl quemaron y destruyeron el templo junto con sus malvados sacerdotes.

Un pequeño puesto al sur del Ikorbân, Gha Nêkha fue construido para proporcionar agua y refugio a los viajeros cansados que navegan por el desierto del sur de Ambarûl. Aunque está cerca de Eshadûr, los Ordâkhai no han mostrado interés en este pequeño asentamiento.

Construido por Númenor durante el reinado de Tar-Telperiën, el muro fue construido como una barrera para proteger su refugio de Vëalondë, ahora Umbar, de los pueblos nativos. El Muro de Telperiën fue destruido por terremotos en la Segunda Edad y más tarde por los Hamâti usando Narghâk cuando conquistaron Umbar.

Los restos de un alto puente arqueado construido en los primeros años de la Tercera Edad para que la Ruta de las Riquezas cruzara el Ikorbân. También conocido como el Tramo de Zibâla, fue destruido por los Ambarûli hace unos cien años en un esfuerzo por mantener a raya a los ejércitos de Ordâkh. Este acto de destrucción solo ralentizó el avance de los Ordâkhai y no los detuvo.
Un huerto de naranjos aún en funcionamiento, este huerto proporciona frutas a Ambarûl, con suficiente excedente para comerciar con las comunidades vecinas.

Hace mucho tiempo se extraía sal de roca de estas minas cuando Ambarûl era un centro de comercio en Shâgana. Los túneles han sido abandonados durante mucho tiempo, ya que los trabajadores se han visto obligados a centrarse en la agricultura para proporcionar alimentos a las tierras menos fértiles controladas por el Imperio de Ordâkh. La mayoría de la gente no se atreve a entrar en las antiguas minas, ya que se sabe que están infestadas de usan-kûni.

Construido sobre pilotes de madera sobre el pantano, Iridír es el principal pueblo de Ambarûl. Hogar de agricultores, pescadores y artesanos, ya no es el centro de comercio que solía ser. Después de liberarse del yugo de sus opresores Ordâkhai, Girhâzi y los demás habitantes de Iridír trabajan para restaurar el comercio en el pueblo mientras mantienen la independencia de Ambarûl.

Situada en la orilla norte del Vado de Algas, Sûru es una fortificación Dumûri que les permite mantener el control del único paso de río en Ambarûl. Las torres de arqueros que se están construyendo en Sûru ayudarán a los Dumûri a defender el paso del río y les permitirán vigilar el camino, protegiendo así a los viajeros y a las caravanas comerciales.

The vaults and tombs of Nirgambâr stand in a sheltered valley in the northern reaches of the Khûd, now largely buried by desert. The tombs were used by Black Númenóreans in the Third Age to house their dead, and the Khûdi say restless spirits and dangerous wights have stalked their silent halls ever since. Rumour has it these occurrences predate even the Black Númenóreans, and may have been involved in their abandonment of the site, but none still live who might say for certain.

The colossal statue Menundâri-en, the Eternal One, was sculpted during the Second Age in memory of the mighty sorcerer-king Izighûz. It was considered heretical by the Church of Barkhûsh, which attempted to destroy it, but what remains of the Eternal One can still be seen in Khûd Zagin.

This valley and cavern complex among the rocky canyons in the east of the Khûd was called 'Thieves' Cut' by the residents of Jirush and their Ordâkhai occupiers. The name was adopted as a badge of honour by the varied brigands, highwaymen, and freedom fighters that now make their home here in the Cut, and they use its Shagâni name of Ghalbûru.

A Khanâg serves as a resting-place for traders and their beasts on the major roads that pass through the desert, and as a meeting-place and market for local residents of the Khûd.
This Khanâg west of Jirush still bustles with moderate activity, despite the soldiers of Ordâkh stationed nearby.

A Khanâg serves as a resting-place for traders and their beasts on the major roads that pass through the desert, and as a meeting-place and market for local residents of the Khûd.
This Khanâg east of Jirush is no longer active, and has become ruined and desolate. Few travel here, and of those who make the journey most have cause to regret it.
In the language of the Shagâni, the name Danagír means 'safe path,' but the high span that bridges the River Barûg between Khûd Zagin and Imhûlar does not feel as safe as its name promises.

Jirush was once the chief town and resupply station for caravans passing south along the Road of Riches, but today it is mostly derelict, its people displaced by war and forced relocation to the mines. Some old men and women remain in Jirush, their hands kept busy with daily troubles even as their minds remember better days, long ago. The sand is slowly overtaking Jirush, and it is a common belief of those few who remain here that in a dozen years or fewer, the town will be entirely consumed by the spreading desert.

In the language of the Avabár-kintai, the name Shonith means 'glade of peace,' and the Elves who tend this oasis in the southern reaches of the Khûd work tirelessly so it may retain that name. The Veróthi of faded Kintai grow on islands in the pool at the centre of Shonith, and others are planted around the water, an oasis of life kept separate from the desert sands... for the time being.

The Ordâkhai presence in Khûd Zagin remains a danger to local residents, despite the heavy losses sustained by soldiers of the Great Southern Empire during the War of the Ring. The Black Serpent will not return from Gondor, but many of those who fought for him fled from the fighting before the walls of Minas Tirith, and they are made even more desperate and dangerous as they return to the lands they claim for their own.

Crebain and carrion birds dwell among the angular structures and rocky cliffs of Nu-hashâr, sheltered from unwanted attention by the steep rise upon which the fortress of Ar-jirush overlooks the Khûd.
Birds nest among the greenery of Anzusag on the cliffs high above the oasis of Shonith. From here the sands of the desert seem far away, a distant mirage.

Er-atûr was once a fertile oasis like the others tended by the Kintai, but it is no longer a place of thriving vegetation and greenery. Now wrathful spirits whisper on the wind and Er-atûr has become a place of ill omen.

The banks of the River Usâl were once green and fertile, but the Great Dearth dried out the fields and left Ish Dâra to fall into ruin and decay. Now only lizards and scorpions call this ruin home, and the Khûdi have left to find a more hospitable dwelling.

The wind whistles through the canyons of Sûr Zugub in the southern reaches of the Khûd, where lizards and other creatures bake on the hot stones. Travellers are advised to keep to the shade provided by the high stones, for the oppressive heat threatens to end any unwise journey.
Wights prowl among the ruins of Ul Sukûd, high above the crypts of Nirgambâr.

The jackals of Shukabad never sleep. They remain alert and aware at all times, padding on quiet feet among the piles of bones and skulls that line their lair, eager to find the next unwary traveller who might become their next meal.

This fortress overlooking the settlement of Jirush still hosts many soldiers of Ordâkh, both from the local garrison and those who escaped the recent Ambarûli liberation. The Ordâkhai keep watch over the road, waylaying passing travellers for the purpose of exacting heavy tolls. The cost of these tolls increases as the temperature rises, as does the threat of the Ordâkhai who collect them.

Hidden deep within war-torn Imhûlar, an Ordâkh-controlled trading post traffics in phials of liquid with a dangerous reputation: water from Tûl Zakana, the Well of Forgetting. Locals advise you steer clear of Tûl Zakana, for many have vanished in its vicinity. Did they run afoul of the Ordâkhai, or did they imbibe too greedily of the waters and lose all sense of themselves?

The Tombs of Esh-kimâkhi, the \qhallows of the three,\q were constructed by Aragín the Queller, first King of Hamât. The triple crypt was built in memory of the three great enemies he slew before sundering his sword and devoting the rest of his life to peace.
This hilltop prominence was carved by the peoples of old Hamât to resemble a lion's head overlooking the dying forests and the lands downstream.

This is the home of Usakâr, an aged hermit who lives in the forest and keeps to the old ways of venerating the guardians of the wood. The extent of his secret knowledge is unknown even to the Kintai, who count themselves among his friends. He despairs over the death of the trees, and hopes there may be some means of reversing the pestilence that consumes them.

Some among the Kintai whisper of Kûgrun, the Golden Sanctuary, a place of peace located somewhere in the dying forest. When pressed, they will hesitate to speak of its true location for reasons of their own.

This tall and timeworn stone bridge crossing the Ikorbân was originally constructed by the Númenóreans as part of their project to channel the river. The name 'Span of Princes' was given to the bridge in honour of two princes of Gondor who fell in battle near this location.

Kûr Anzar is a fortified town built among the ruins of a Númenórean citadel that was itself constructed on the bones of an ancient Khandari stronghold. This was originally the ruling seat of the Shâr of Hamât, but centuries of civil warfare and invasion from Gondor have laid waste to it. Now Kûr Anzar is mainly held by the Ordâkhai remnant and cultists who serve the Church of the All-seeing.

The town of Urmâkh in western Imhûlar has become home to many of the Shagâni residents displaced from Kûr Anzar. Their anger at the soldiers of Ordâkh is matched, if not exceeded, by their hatred for the despots of Gondor who feature prominently in the tales and legends of their land.

The boars of Shakhdag have not escaped the pestilence that holds Imhûlar in its grip.

The Curthádi spirits that haunt Róthirin were born from the sickness and death that claimed the woods where a living Kinta faded into one of the Vairi. Now these spirits serve the Dark Lord Sauron, despite his recent defeat.

Wights stalk the crypts of Adakûr, the outermost reaches of the graveyard that also contains the triple tomb built by Aragín the Queller before he walked the path of peace. The names of the ancient ones buried in Adakûr are not as well-known as the three great enemies for whom Aragín constructed Esh-kimâkhi.
Some creatures, like the bog-lurkers of Zahûmakh, remain hardy enough to survive among the pools in south-east Imhûlar, despite the pestilence that endangers the woods.
The Ordâkhai threaten the woods nearby from their hidden encampment of Ghât Lor, among the rocks in south-eastern Imhûlar.
Crebain flit over the pools of Ghât Okho in eastern Imhûlar, but the fish they seek to claim have succumbed to disease and pestilence.
Servals stalk among the rubble that might once have housed residents of Urmâkh, but the people have long since fled and their home is now a ruin.
A band of Orcs has set up camp at Tharháth to watch the road leading north out of Imhûlar by way of the Bridge of Princes.

Orcs have claimed this street in Kûr Anzar for their own. Despite the fall of Sauron, they still maintain their allegiance to the Church of the All-seeing and provide what aid they can to the cultists of Barkhûsh.

Cultists of Barkhûsh serve the Church of the All-seeing from Dûl Zidur, north-east of Kûr Anzar, with instructions to meet here in the event anything harms their hold upon the central city of Imhûlar.

The scorpions at Mûr Igam dwell in the shadow of Kûr Anzar, and it appears they have not troubled the soldiers and cultists who now occupy the city. Should that change, each side may find itself unprepared to overcome the challenge posed by the other.

There is beauty even in death, for at Urgudag flowers grow among the bone-piles assembled by the ravenous jackals of western Urash Dâr.
The jackals of Khazâda have grown more bold in recent days, endangering the travellers who find they must travel in eastern Urash Dâr.
The high canyon walls on either side of Khûn Sagaz ensure that any foolhardy enough to venture within have little hope of escaping the watchful gaze of the Orcs who dwell here.
Deep within Sar-kidul, the Orcs have been kept busy fashioning great machines of war and training for the day they will be loosed upon the rest of the Ikorbân Valley.
The encampment of Ab-dâna gives to the Orcs a view of much of the rest of Urash Dâr, providing a vantage point from which they can make their deadly plans for war.

Orcs have overtaken the stone keep of Maurûsh and pushed out the former Ordâkhai residents. From this defensible position, the Orcs can strike almost any location in Urash Dâr with very little warning.

Not content to remain within the dark cave where they were born, the scorpions of Dul Râkh boiled into the canyon outside. The scorpions overran the Orcs foolishly camped outside the cave mouth, and now the canyon belongs to them.

This ancient hermitage was built into the walls of a narrow, spring-fed gap where greenery thrives despite the arid climate. It was once the retreat of poets and philosophers, but that was long ago; in the years since it held a trove of secret lore, generations of robbers and brigands have used it to store their own plunder.
Tangled webs woven by the spiders that lurk at Ushbarab make travel in north-western Urash Dâr difficult, if not outright impossible.

The filthy and dangerous beasts known as kergrim have fashioned a lair among the rocks below the cliffside fortress of Ashâgir. The Shagâni call this place Tûkurdul, the 'gnaw-heap,' and no other name could best it.

Few alone remain at Ilzag Khûl, for evil stirs in nearby Maurûsh. Now it must become a place of safety from which your allies can strike against the foes that endanger all of Urash Dâr.
In the Shagâni language, Shengarâsh means 'encampment of the rain or mist;' it is truly an appropriate name for this camp by the Falls of Ilûritu in northern Urash Dâr.

This great stonework was constructed by the Númenóreans when they channeled the Ikorbân River near Urash Dâr. The process took many years, but its end result broadened the waterway and made it more navigable for Númenórean ships passing inland.
These falls in northern Urash Dâr are beautiful and perilous, and none know what secrets they may conceal.

Hidden deep within the gorge-lands, the clifftop fortress of Ashâgir was built into a high outcrop well above the canyon floor. Once a lift climbed to the heights, but that device has been long-since destroyed; now only precipitous paths wind slowly to the lofty entrance. The last king of Hamât sheltered within when the Great Southern Empire of Ordâkh invaded, but he commanded the destruction of the fortress rather than surrender it, and perished there. Now Ashâgir stands empty, plundered of its treasure.

Sûr Akil, the north-eastern canyon through which the River Mûshid runs, means 'the gorge of woe' in the language of the Shagâni. None remember why they gave it this name, but the sensation of great evil that has settled upon this area in recent days seems justification enough.

The way-station of Malgâma attracts all sorts, or at least, it would if there was still a large population remaining in the settlements of Urash Dâr. Instead, the folk who come to this small collection of buildings near Zikrum-dûl share one thing in common: their eccentricity.

Recent quakes ripped open a fissure in a formerly-solid cliff face, altering the course of the river and revealing the doorstep of Utug-bûr, a stone structure kept secret for untold years. None still live who remember the making of this place, and now a sensation of great evil grips the hearts of any who approach.

Tûl Zakana, the Well of Forgetting -- Tier 1

Deep in the war-torn lands of Imhûlar, locals warn you of an Ordâkhai encampment, a trading post of sorts. It is known as Tûl Zakana, the Well of Forgetting, whose waters will make you forget your troubles, and, if you drink enough, even who you are. But unless you are trading for this water, it's best to stay well clear of the Well, for many have vanished near it, never to be seen again. You are now tasked by the families of the vanished with investigating the Well and its secrets.

Find Nisigurûm
Providing the Ekhamâti a toehold into the fertile lands of Ambarûl, Garash Kâru sits on a commanding hilltop outside the southern Ambarûli marshes.

The Ekhamâti have established crude fortifications and a rudimentary encampment outside a set of pits in northern Khûd Zagin. Few know what they are searching for there, and whether they should fear what they find.

Dun Shûma, the King's Fortress, has long been rumoured to contain treasures of the Kings of Nisaka, an ancient dynasty of the Khûd. More recently, rumours suggest that artifacts of Aragín the Queller, famed ancient uniter of Shagâna and King of Hamât have spread, causing many to try their luck at finding these relics of the revered Aragín.

Nisigurûm, or the \qgreen-watch\q, was once part of a flourishing collection of human encampments in Nisigím, \qthe emerald wood\q. Now the name is tinged in sorrow, as the woods surrounding Nisigurûm have surrendered to the Pale Blight, and the corrupting influence of the Ordâkhai, who now control Nisigurûm. The Ordâkhai at Nisigurûm are themselves commanded by the Shâr of Ekhamât, the cruel Bârshud II.
The high canyon walls form natural barriers and impediments to assault at Az Shûdai, providing an extra advantage to the Ordâkhai and Ekhamâti who dwell there.

The Jewel of Mûr Ghala, Zajâna is a city of trade and knowledge. Located at a fortuitous junction along the Great Road, Zajâna serves both Umbar and points further south, acting as a great connector. Zajâna was recently freed from the grip of the empire of Ordâkh, although the Jewelled Council loyal to Ordâkh still control a portion of Zajâna. The Doorwards have reestablished the rule of Zajâna by the Zajâni people following the Blue Mutiny, and rule over most of the city as a council of equals.
Trade is in the air and culture of Zajâna, and traders far and wide come to the great city to ply their wares and make their fortunes. Elsewhere the Pohâni scholars work and research in the Kalmakhíla, the great library in Zajâna where much of the knowledge of Mûr Ghala is stored.

A fertile fishing village, Sen Chatâk is located along the White-wrath river. A formerly peaceful village, Sen Chatâk has recently seen its troubled magnified with both brigand and goblin attacks, puncturing its once tranquil and friendly veneer.

Orange groves that the locals of Sormedân keep and watch over. The groves do well in the clay soil of Sormedân, producing enough fruit that Sormedân farmers sell the excess both to Zajâna and other nearby towns.
Khamósh-engar is where the locals of Sormedân bury their dead. Those buried here have their moments of death rendered in steles, carved stones which depict the moment and manner of their death.

A modest-sized town, Ingar-garâsh has been abandoned in the battle between the Doorwards and the Jewelled Council over Zajâna. A large force of Ordâkhai loyal to the Jewelled Council are situated near Ingar-garâsh. Recently Shâra Mizâdi has established an encampment in Ingar-garâsh, and is striking out at the nearby Ordâkhai forces in her pursuit of the villainous Bârshud II.

A fabled set of caves located outside of Zajâna, fabulous wealth is rumoured to exist within the caves. Locals say a powerful curse is attached to those who enter the caves however, so few make their way inside. Recently an infamous brigand named Bârlat the Bold has made the caves his home, from which he strikes at merchants and travellers on the nearby Great Road.

One of many markets within Zajâna, the Larinâsta is where many characters both savoury and unsavoury come to conduct their business. Much is bought and sold within the Larinâsta. Some of it is even legal.
The great library of Zajâna, the Kalmakhíla is a vast repository containing much of the knowledge gathered within Mûr Ghala.

Sormedân means \qred soil\q in the native Zajâni, so called for the village's red, clay-like soil. This soil has proven quite fertile, and results in Sormedân and its surrounds nurturing much of Kighân with its rich orchards and grain fields. The locals also keep cattle and bees, although there have been disturbances with both recently. The elders of Sormedân also keep a watchful eye on nearby Adagím. The sickness gripping Adagím has recently spilled over, and threatens to bespoil Sormedân's natural bounty.

The bees of Medân Makhai once worked with the farmers of Sormedan. The farmers built them structures and kept them safe from predators and cold, and in return took a portion of the bees' honey. Recently, however, a new queen has caused the bees to become aggressive, unlike themselves, and they have savagely attacked and stung the farmers attempting to tend to them.
The savage jázgai make their camp near the water hole of Dân Shatagan. Locals whisper of their savagery, and especially that of their matriarch and leader, whom they have named Bloodtooth.

Khatzâla is the roost of the eccentric birds known as the kalorkhûn. The kalorkhûn can be quite aggressive when disturbed. Some have been domesticated and used as show animals, although only by the bravest and most adventurous of the Zajâni.

A large encampment of Ordâkhai outside of Zajâna, this is where much of the military might of the Jewelled Council remains. Once the Blue Mutiny occurred, the Ordâkhai within the city were forced either within the Halls of Lajór within Zajâna, or outside of it and into Jag Golód. Here the Ordâkhai plot their next move, and attempt to retake Zajâna from their hated enemy, the Doorwards of Zajâna.

The former imperial palace of Zajâna, this is where Khastakhól of the Jewelled Council remains and holds court. The Jewelled Council, a shadow government of the empire of Ordâkh, once held sway over Zajâna but was recently overthrown by the people of Zajâna in the Blue Mutiny. Now the Jewelled Council controls only the Hall and its immediate surroundings. Although wounded, it is still a danger to strike out and reclaim all of Zajâna for Ordâkh.

The blight afflicting Adagím has taken root in Shádhag, just over the border in Kighân. Locals call it \qthe Moulder-grove\q as the plants begin to rot and decay in the once fertile grove. Strange and violent trees have taken over Shádhag and made it their own, striking at nearby Sormedân villagers in recent days.

A pall hangs over the air of Bâdrasag, also known as the Blade-horn. Once a fortress to Second Age evils, the Blade-horn now sits empty. Locals stay well clear of it, whispering of strange spirits and haunting sounds that penetrate the night air outside its environs. What secrets could be hiding within, and what further evils might the Blade-horn be sheltering?
The lush grasslands of Kighân are the perfect environs for the graceful and swift oryx, who make the fields of Sâkhazai their home.

The twisting and dark caves of Jâr Obadal have proven a welcome environment for cave spiders. In recent months Jâr Obadal has been claimed by Jûkhtar the Ravenous and her prodigious brood. They strike out at nearby patrols and unlucky travellers, bringing them back to the dark caves where they leash them with silk and twist them into ready meals.
Located near the Great Road, Pazakhêra is home to many thieves, pick-pockets and rapscallions eager to feast on the riches of the merchant caravans travelling along the Great Road.

The Hold of Jalkhíla is where a group of hardened brigands make their camp. From here, they strike out at the nearby village of Sen Chatâk along with those travelling the Great Road on their way to or from Zajâna.

Hurum Kâna is fabled for its treasure caves, which many Zajâni claim possess huge treasure caches. However, none who enter Hurum Kâna have ever been seen again. Until recently, when a self-styled brigand king, Bârlat the Bold, has made Hurum Kâna his home. Travellers who escape with their lives claim to have seen Bârlat and his gang of brigands adorned with gold and gemstones of both weight and variety that can scarcely be believed.

Glúkroz was once a simple rock outcropping. Now goblins have made it their home, striking out at the nearby village of Sen Chatâk on vicious raids. The goblins are taking food, cleaving innocent villagers and setting fire to their homes.

The marshes of Charganpâta proved a fertile breeding ground for zizani, fierce biting insects of great size. For that reason, many steer well clear of Charganpâta and its belligerent insect inhabitants.

An ancient hall of the Temámir dwarves, Jiret-menêsh has been home to dwarves since the First Age. At various points throughout history, they have been allied with the Kintai, Nêshak, Zajâna, and the Temámir of the Shoreward Stone in Umbar, among others. Following the razing of Lâkindar and the subsequent Din of Stone, Châmelek Gêta, Lord of Jiret-menêsh, ordered the closing of the doors, cutting Jiret-menêsh off from the outside world for the next one hundred years, only to re-open when the threats of the Ordâkhai and Barkhûshim have passed.

Khanâg Gur is the last remaining khanâg still operating in An Shêru, though many merchants and travellers still don't consider it a safe place to rest. An outlaw gang called the Khanda-khêl, or 'the Laughing Ones', currently controls the khanâg. Their leader, or 'Mashár', is a man named Halshûm, who welcomes visitors as long as they spend coin during their stay. Those who do not spend enough coin often find themselves robbed on the road following their visit.

Gadim-ûn, or the Hallows of Gadim, is an ancient necropolis overlooking the White-wrath River from on high in the north-eastern reaches of An Shêru. The once desolate boneyard now serves as the hiding place of the Jatsakóri, escaped Shagâni thralls desperate to save their friends and family members from Ordâkhai bondage. In recent months, the corpses of Gadim-ûn have been awakened by some dark craft.

Ogultáth is a dense patch of forest now known to the Kintai as \qspider-hollow\q. The blight in the land has corrupted the spiders here and heightened their aggression as they expand their webs further into the land.

The Kintai call this place the weaver's house as Dathrudúsh has been home to the spiders who dwell deep in the marsh for many years. The roots of the mother tree now push the blight out from the earth and taint the creatures here.

The spiders of Narchásh have earned the name given to them by the Kintai. The hole of rending as it is known, due to their vicious nature of preying on travellers unfortunate enough to step through their webs. The spiders now rotten with blight spread the poison across the land to weaken their potential targets.

Known as the vale of the devourers, the spiders of Thalat Tîr fester with rot as it blooms from the Hill of the Mother herself, tainting the earth and creature alike. Here the spiders are well known to the people of Adagím and grow monstrous as they lie in wait for any to pass by.

The rocky pits of Chortáth are scattered with bones and corpses that belonged to any who venture too deep. It is home to a large pack of jackals who have taken hold of the land, using the maze-like rocks to stalk their prey. The Kinta scouts of Sâr Marsag regularly fight with the beasts to try and gain the upper hand in safeguarding the roads.

Now known as Mauthark, the forest near the borders of Adagím and Imhular has become a home to Orcs who roam the marsh as the lone allies of the Ordâkhi willing to tolerate the vile conditions as they threaten the borders of the few remaining groves of the Kintai.

The trees of Hadrudád have not felt the pain of the blight as much as other place in Adagím with green still visible on the earth, but it has not been immune. The trees here still fester with rot and have become deadly for travellers. The scouts of Sâr Marsag to the east hold them at bay as they keep the roads to Kighân safe.

Mokh Grazádh has become a stronghold for Orcs in the sickened marsh of Adagím. With its central location in the forest the Orcs here terrorize the Kintai along with any travellers who dare tread these roads. The threat they pose to the Elves grows by the day as their attention is turned towards the Pale Blight.

Lhámuth is home to many lurkers of the marsh. Once a serene grouping of ponds, now poisoned and deadly from the rot in the earth. In recent years the tainted monstrosities that grew from the wood-trolls have begun to roam these lands, disrupting the bog-lurkers as the blight consumes them.

Named the Lair of the Shadlúgai, the marsh here still holds some green within its waters as they are far from the thick forest and the roots of the mother tree. The Kintai speak of the stone-worms who live here, skulking in the water for any prey that comes too close to their jaws.

Found along the path to Sul Madásh is Saig Hathíl, the blade-hives in the common tongue. Home to sickleflies seeking out any place they can to avoid the rot. The small patch of green within the marsh that survives through the will of the Kintai has become their nesting grounds until the Pale Blight closes in.

The trees of Hordírid have grown fierce and dangerous with the spreading rot in Adagím. The patch of land known by locals as the Wokenhurst is now a warning to travellers seeking to venture into the northern parts of the forest.

The first camp built by the Orcs when they came to Adagím. Fushaum Sûlm is a stronghold deep enough in the marshes that they do not get many attackers but fortified to withstand them all the same. The Orcs use it to scout the Kintai who guard the road into Kighân as well as attack any travellers who try and slip by.

Dur Nâgu, or the 'fortress of the island', is the ruins of an ancient Nêshakari fortress and ship-yard, where they once built river boats and launched them along the river Agâl. In recent days, it has become the secret haven of thralls escaping from the prison Esh Mêkag.

The Dawn-warden is a giant statue of the ancient hero-king of Nísaka, Izighûz Menûndari. Unlike its twin in Khûd Zagin, this statue is mostly intact. The advance troops of Aradûn have recently made it their camp in preparation for their invasion of Idagâl, to reclaim the region from the Ordâkhai. Unfortunately, they have learned too late that the statue is haunted by a mysterious force, known to the local people as Ishími, the Anguished Wind.
Nashûbu is the secret camp of Shâra Mizâdi's forces in a hidden alcove at the base of the cliffs beneath Emax Dûl. Here, there is said to be a secret way to breach the defences the enemy city.
The Hamâti Forward Camp serves as Mizâdi's foothold into Idagâl, where she will eventually launch an attack on the fortress of Emax Dûl and push the Ordâkhai from Mûr Ghala.

Ahâba, or the 'well of the barrens', is a lush oasis and home of the Beltáni people. After decades of attempted subjugation by the Ordâkh Empire, the ancient people are slow to trust outsiders, but for those that earn that trust, it is a beautiful reprieve from the harsh conditions of Idagâl.

Sâr Marsag, the last camp on the road into Kighân, is held by the scouts of Adagím as a bastion within the rotting forest. They keep their bonfire burning to provide a beacon to travellers that they will be safe here as the battle against the Pale Blight rages on.

An ancient wonder from before the Din of Stone carved into the mountainside in Adagím. The structure was being built by a ruler who wanted to make his mark on this world known as Nagakhêdi. The wonder was left unfinished and sealed off long ago.
The Kintai of the woods have left the structure untouched for years as they saw it as a futile effort from the start even now calling it the \qFool's Descent\q, and their eyes have been turned towards safeguarding their groves against the blight that rages in their lands. The sealed door has cracks in its stone and a foul air leaks out from within.

Tûl Ama, known as the Hill of the Mother, is an outcropping where once grew a giant holm-oak, one of the oldest in Shagâna, called the Old Mother in tale and song. It is now dying, the fungal rot rising up its massive trunk and causing it to weep bloody sap as its leaves blacken and wither.
The hill's warden, Irsinith, has communed with the tree for centuries and speaks on her behalf, though the tree's affliction has left her sickly and wracked with grief.

A Kinta grove, hitherto unspoiled, that has begun to succumb to the Pale Blight. The tender of the grove, a hermit named Tálbiral, has razed the forest around the grove in an attempt to form a barrier from the rot.

The dale of beauty as it is known in the native Kintár. Sul Madásh is the chief grove-settlement of Adagím. A green sanctuary overlooking the devastation, tucked among cascading streams within a fold of the eastern Mûr, but the infection can only be contained for so long while the Elves' numbers continue to decline.
The chieftains of Sul Madásh, a wedded pair – Ildimár the husband, Dáthlil the wife – have thus far kept the Pale Blight at bay but know the battle will soon be lost. Defiant to the end, they intend to go down fighting.

A hilltop in eastern An Shêru called Sang Luzûkh in Shagâni. It serves as the den for a large pack of jázgai, creatures known for scavenging, but who will attack if threatened or if food is scarce.

Once a lush and verdant grove of the Kintai, this hilltop is now a refuge for bandits and other outlaws amidst a dry and rocky desert. The Elves are now gone, but several Veróthi, the trees that remain when an Elf has reached Trothúl, still linger.

An abandoned mine called Erakúndo by the Ordâkhi. It was last used in the time of Shurash Hûl, the emperor of Ordâkh, who led his armies north into Shagâna, destroying the Usâl River and much of the Mûr. This site is now home to feral mûmakil, beasts of burden who have survived or escaped the wars of Men.
The roosting place of Kalorkhûn, terrifying birds of unusual size, who made their home at the height of the sky. Some say they taste like chicken.

Acidic hot springs in northern An Shêru, called Shêgarim by the locals, have boiled to the surface since the Din of Stone. While the water here can burn or kill most animals, rock-worms have found the superheated, acrid water to be to their liking.

Acidic hot springs in southern An Shêru that have boiled to the surface since the Din of Stone. While the water here can burn or kill most animals, rock-worms have found the superheated, acrid water to be to their liking.

Near the head of the Usâl River, a rupture in the mountainside reveals the entrance to Damudûr, a First Age stronghold of the Thardúth. These caverns that once housed the breeding pits of the Utúgi have been hidden by sorcery since the time of Morgoth's defeat, and are now once again revealed. What dangers lie within, and what threats have already come forth?
A crypt only a short distance south of the ancient necropolis of Gadim-ûn, something has disturbed the dead, causing their decayed bodies to leave the tombs and wander the land.
This mountain-top at the height of the sky is home to a colony of rocs, called anzûri in Shagâna, giant birds that are as hostile as they are huge.
An outpost of the Ordâkhai of Shêru, from here they dispatch patrols and attempt to maintain control of the western side of the region.
Called Modan Rôkh in Ordâkhai, the Beast-fields are named for the sûlokil you will usually find there.
One must be either very brave or very foolish to enter Uruthúsh, as it is home to a band of fearsome Utûgi, Orcs given life in the Elder Days by Morgoth's dark craft.
This arching bridge is all that remains of these long-forgotten ruins in western An Shêru. It is now home to a band of kergrim who scavenge the remains of the victims of this harsh environment.
Gredbyg have lived on these rocky slopes as long as anyone can remember. Some say they have been here since before the land was ravaged and An Shêru was still green and forested.

Instead of skilfully mining into the mountain, the Ordâkhai have their enthralled Jatsakóri workers excavating an open pit, forever scarring the land. This practice is detested by the Temámir of Shêru, and was banned when the Men of Nísaka swore the peace-bringing Oath of Jiret-menêsh, in which several mines in An Shêru were surrendered to Men so long as they swore ever to honour and respect the land from which they took their bounty, and never to cut stone except with the greatest care.

Kôth Rau, the centre of Ordâkhai activity in An Shêru, is situated on a slope and encompasses the entrance to Damudûr. Taking orders from a coven of Bokhóri sorceresses, the soldiers here are zealots who deny the defeat of Barkhûsh and await his return. There is also an Utûgi presence in the camp, as well as prisoners who are taken and questioned for unknown reasons.

In the days of old, Lâkindar was a prosperous mine of the Temámir dwarves. Now, however, it is commonly called 'The Quelling-house' due to its more recent use by the invading armies of Ordâkh. After brutally stamping out resistance in An Shêru, the mine was used as an execution chamber and dumping ground for the bodies of dissenters. It is also said that the Priests of Barkhûsh ritually sacrificed many an innocent dwarf in this unhappy place, adding to its unnerving reputation. To make matters worse, in recent months, the corpses of The Quelling-house have been awakened by some dark craft.

Explore enemy camps, settlements, and lairs in An Shêru in Mûr Ghala.
Part of an ancient necropolis of Gadim-ûn, overlooking the White-wrath River. Many of the dead here have awakened from their graves in recent months, their rest disturbed by some dark sorcery.

Shahûru, or 'shrine on a summit', is all that remains of an ancient Nêshak temple where the local people left offerings, praying for abundant harvests and the blessings of rain. The identity of the being the Mûr folk prayed to is lost to time, but indications are that they were female.

Ushumût, or the Grave of Serpents, is the remains of three massive dragons and home to the wild-drakes of Idagâl. The Beltáni have passed down the tale of the fall of these dragons, named Ahûshu, Nuzêru, and Rabûg. They say that Shurug-nîn, the mythical hero of the First Age, struck them down, and their bodies fell into the lake where they rested for many thousands of years. It was only relatively recently that the Din of Stone drained the lake and revealed the dragons' grave to the world.

The Wither-watch, or Okhatohól, was once a thriving Shagâni town overlooking the river Agâl. The Din of Stone, the drying of the lake, and the invasion by the Ordâkhai slowly left the town nearly abandoned, as people fled for a better life. In recent years, the Ordâkhai have completely taken over the town, to use it as a northern base to launch raids. The few remaining residents were taken and never seen again.

Jolakhúro, or 'notch of the tunnel', is the Ordâkhai forward camp that watches the road to their main fortress at Emax Dûl. The soldiers there watch for approaching enemies, and are the first sent out in response to trouble elsewhere in Idagâl.

Emax Dûl, 'high hall of the cleft', or the High-hold, is an ancient fortress that has stood through the rise and fall of the many dynasties of both Nêshak and Nísaka. It is now the seat of power of the Ordâkhai in Mûr Ghala, and home to the royal family of the crown prince of the empire.

Karmu Râx, or 'the mound of the turtles', is the gathering place for many dread-tortoises along the trickle that remains of the river Agâl. The shallow water and shelter provided by old wrecks from ships beached by the Din of Stone prove a suitable environment for the reptiles.

The Scardelve, or 'Góbor-noti', is the remains of an old pit mine carved from the cliff by the Ordâkhai. Once the ore ran dry, it became a holding pen for Mûmakil. As the Ordâkhai began to lose control of the region following their loss at the Battle of Pelennor Fields, they too lost control of the mûmakil housed in the mine. The great beasts now run wild across all of Idagâl.

Khâb Ishil, or 'the tomb of shards', is the ancient burial house of heroes from the kingdoms of Nêshak and Nísaka. It was long ago sealed and left untouched for hundreds of years. The Din of Stone shook the earth and opened the tomb, allowing the kergrim to enter, defile it, and make it their nest.

Esh Mêkag, 'the Silent Mouth', is an ancient Nêshakari fortress built into the stone cliffs of the Mûr. In recent years, the Ordâkhai have turned the fortress into a horrific prison and work-camp. The priests of Barkhûsh oversee the subjugation of people from all over Shagâna, who become thralls to the empire.

Kidu-bâla, or 'rebel-covert', is a cliff-side camp of brigands and Ordâkhai deserters who have declared independence from the laws of both the empire and any upstart kingdoms who claim dominion over Idagâl. They prey on desperate travellers and steal the meager resources the local Beltáni people have.
The brigands at Duríga, or 'gleaners' cleft', survive by assaulting Ordâkhai patrols and stealing the rations from the escaped thralls hiding in the ruins of Dur Nâgu.

Gnasher's Delf, or 'Haraz Hûr', is just the top of a large grodbog hive. They thrive in the cliffs because of deep cracks in the rock that lead to ground water, opened by the Din of Stone over a hundred years ago.

Nax Shalâl, or 'the Slithering Pit', is a recessed oasis, hidden in the cliffs. What would be a refuge for the people of Idagâl has become too dangerous to go near, as the local cobra population has exploded in size.

'Kasâshu the Grinder? There is no gift you could give me to make me approach that frightening creature, friend. You would think a turtle would move slowly, but not Kasâshu!' -Malgârzor of Ahâba
'Some snakes are not dangerous. But these snakes are not Ershubât!' -Dimûzga the Wayfarer
Akílu the Feaster would swoop from the sky with deadly speed and carry away the carcasses of creatures slain by larger predators, but now she has become the meal and will feast no more.
The lizard Gírkhash was known to eat creatures more than double or triple his own size. The secret to this capability of his? Patience.
'Could one creature really have birthed so many gredbyg? I do not want to think of it!' -Kindrígi the Wayfarer
'Mórobul! The earth shudders beneath his every step! He is my favourite, I confess it. Let all beware if he ever turns his anger upon us!' -Shâdugan Gânda
Súlkhor the Hollow-hearted, an Utûgi sorcerer skilled in dark arts, was stationed in Emax Dûl until he was finally slain. To his last day he worked his cruel sorceries on behalf of a foul mistress.
Once a soldier of Ordâkh, Brikóno turned to banditry and worked to fill his own pockets rather than those of the Hûl. Death caught him before the anger of his distant emperor reached Brikóno.

The mighty drake Imtushâl the Gall-spitter stalked Idagâl and preyed upon creatures and people caught out in the open or beside the dry lakebed for many years. If the blood of ancient dragons ran still in Imtushâl's veins, it has been spilt.

Track down and defeat every formidable enemy in Kighân.
Korutásh had a fell reputation for nastiness even among others of his kind, and you have done well to put an end to his reign of cruelty in Kighân.

Kighân is much less forested than Adagím to the north, but Nâralarg still proved frighteningly adept at catching people unawares. The folk of Sormedân will sleep more soundly now that you have bested the threatening tree-that-moves.
Jûkhtar was rarely seen... by the living. Now she will be seen even less often, for she is dead.
While neither as large nor as vicious as her mother Bloodtooth, Shahâk was no less dangerous. The people of Zajâna are safer for your efforts.
Even when compared to others of the Kalorkhûn, Târchakh's deadly talons were legendary for their sharpness and the speed with which she could use them against her prey.

Todôkha was the largest and most intimidating of the oryxes that dwelt in Kighân, and ferociously territorial. Many were the innocent travellers along Mûr Ghala who fell beneath the trampling hooves of Todôkha, but no longer.
Villagers of Sormedân reported hearing the buzzing call of the zizanu Lemûlkhan from miles away, at any time of day or night. Such reports have now ended, as has the threat posed by the great insect.
The Tarsâri operative Khamôsh has reached the end of his service. In life, the \qSilent One\q asked no questions of those who selected his enemies. He keeps his quiet even now, in death.

Bloodtooth's many pups harry travellers all throughout Kighân, and their numbers are so great they must do so for many years to come in their deadly mother's memory... but Bloodtooth herself has reached her own hunt's end.
